subtopic: SMUGGLING ACTIVITIES OF CANADIANS ON INTERNATIONAL COMMISSIONS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: SMUGGLING ACTIVITIES OF CANADIANS ON INTERNATIONAL COMMISSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it had been the hope of the government, in view of Canada's important international commitments in Indochina and the extremely delicate situation prevailing there at this time, that the allegations regarding smuggling activities by certain Canadians serving on the international control commissions there would not be made the subject of public debate. Meantime with regard to the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and also by the Minister of National Defence matters that are under investigation are under ordinary circumstances not subject to discussion in parliament, and it has been regarded as a matter of public policy that they ought not to be. However, an hon. member of this house who is not present at the moment, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier), has chosen not to accept the statements of the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the house and has made certain statements outside this house which are inaccurate. For that reason it becomes necessary in the national interest to set the record straight.
Late last year it was discovered that some of the military members of the Canadian delegation to the international supervisory commissions in Indo-China were engaged in smuggling activities within Indo-China. Immediate investigations by the military authorities in Indo-China indicated that one commissioned officer and one non-commissioned officer had engaged in gold smuggling, and five other ranks appeared to have engaged in either the smuggling of gold or opium. All of those involved who were still in Indo-China were recalled to Canada. Disciplinary action was taken in Indo-China against a number of these military personnel before their return to Canada. Investigations of the others are still continuing.
At first it was believed that only military members were involved, but subsequently it was learned that two members of the clerical staff of the Department of External Affairs serving in Indo-China had also been engaged
in smuggling. Administrative action to prevent a recurrence was taken immediately by the Department of External Affairs and by the Department of National Defence. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police were apprised of this situation and were requested to take charge of the investigation in so far as it affected the civilian members of the Department of External Affairs. The two members of the Department of External Affairs engaged in these improper activities were returned to Canada and have been interviewed by the R.C.M.P. They have signed statements admitting that they acted together in smuggling a quantity of gold and a parcel of opium, on behalf of a Chinese person, from one city to another in Indo-China. Both men have been suspended from the public service of Canada with a view to subsequent dismissal.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has referred to ugly rumours and speculation in the press. Three rumours that caused the house most concern appear to have originated in what the hon. gentleman is reported to have said. Reports have appeared in the press that the persons concerned received large sums of money as a result of engaging in these activities. Certain of those concerned did receive sums of money in local currency, but the reports concerning the amounts have been very greatly exaggerated.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam is quoted in the March 9 edition of the Ottawa Citizen as saying:
Viet Nam has been a major source of supply for narcotics coming into Canada.
There is no evidence whatever, Mr. Speaker, that narcotics have been smuggled into Canada by Canadians serving on the three truce commissions in Indo-China. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has linked this affair with what he describes as "mass arrests in British Columbia by Royal Canadian Mounted Police a few months ago." Again I must say that on the information I have- and I have personally looked into the matter in detail-that statement is completely mistaken. There has been nothing to indicate or suggest that this matter is in any way related to the arrests in British Columbia to which the hon. member referred. The drug involved in the matter which is before the house is opium, which the enforcement officers advise is rarely if ever handled by illegal narcotics dealers in Canada.

External Affairs
The statement I have made represents the results of an investigation made not only by the department of defence in respect of those who belong to the armed forces, but as well by the Department of External Affairs and the R.C.M.P. with respect to the civilian employees. If the hon. member, or any hon. member, is in possession of any information bearing on this case, the house may be sure that the information will be used, and used effectively if it is conveyed without delay to those responsible for these investigations. But as far as the government and the several departments are concerned, I have given a full and complete statement regarding this matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: SMUGGLING ACTIVITIES OF CANADIANS ON INTERNATIONAL COMMISSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is well that the Prime Minister should have made this statement. The details of the statement, which will certainly require consideration, seem to me to confirm our view that it would have been well if a statement of this kind had been made immediately after the original allegations were made, because in the very nature of things those allegations were bound1 to receive a great deal of publicity. That happened and that publicity grew, in the absence of information, over the week end in a way which was bound to result in unfortunate speculation and rumours which might have reacted unjustly and unfavourably on the services concerned.
I think the house welcomes the statement made by the Prime Minister, and it is to be hoped this statement will remove some of the more alarming rumours and will put this matter in perspective.

subtopic: SMUGGLING ACTIVITIES OF CANADIANS ON INTERNATIONAL COMMISSIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the members of this group appreciate the Prime Minister's frank statement on this very serious situation, which no doubt has caused great concern to the Canadian people. All I wish to say is that if after investigation these allegations prove to have some substance, the members of the armed forces or personnel of the Department of External Affairs should be dealt with under the Criminal Code and, if proven guilty, sentenced according to Canadian law. We hope there will be no shielding of anyone because of their position or because of the circumstances in which these alleged irregularities existed.

speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Agriculture I should like to make a statement concerning the international wheat agreement.
In January of this year the Canadian government received an invitation from the secretary general of the United Nations to

participate in the United Nations wheat conference, commencing on January 31 in Geneva, for the renewal or replacement of the current international wheat agreement which came into effect on August 1, 1959, and which expires on July 31, 1962.
Mindful of the important part successive wheat agreements have played since the late 1940's in assuring supplies of wheat to importing countries and markets for wheat to exporting countries at equitable and stable prices, and aware of the wide support for the international wheat agreement among producers organizations in western Canada, the government authorized the dispatch of a strong delegation including government officials, Canadian wheat board representatives and members of the advisory committee of the Canadian wheat board, who are at the same time leaders of the principal farm organizations in western Canada.
Nearly 60 countries took part in or were represented by observers at the six week conference. The negotiations have now come to a successful conclusion. Subject to ratification by the governments concerned, a new three year international wheat agreement, similar in structure to the 1959 agreement, will come into force next August 1, expiring on July 31, 1965. Should all the major exporters participating in the conference, including the U.S.S.R., ratify the agreement, all the important sources of wheat will be brought within the ambit of international wheat co-operation.
The new price range raises the minimum price, in U.S. dollars, for No. 1 Northern in store Fort William/Port Arthur and Vancouver from $1.50 to $1.62 and the maximum price from $1.90 to $2.02J. At the current rate of exchange this price range in Canada in dollars is $1.71J minimum and $2.13f maximum. It should be noted that selling prices for the next three years are to be within the price range, and that actual prices will depend on market conditions. It is worth pointing out in this connection that the actual selling price in Canadian dollars for No. 1 Northern at Fort William fell, during the course of the present agreement, to a low of $1.63f in November 1960. This is not only 50 cents lower than the new maximum of almost $2.14, but it is about 8 cents lower than the new minimum.
In view of these facts hon. members will appreciate the remarkable degree to which prices have recovered, due both to a changed market situation and to the current discount on the Canadian dollar. Members will also appreciate the significance of a higher minimum price, keeping in mind the extent to which prices did fall in recent years before
International Wheat Agreement surpluses began to diminish rapidly in the face of increased exports and reduced production.
The new agreement provides that so long as prices remain below the maximum price specified in the agreement, each member importing country undertakes to purchase from member exporting countries a specified percentage of its total commercial purchases of wheat. The exporting countries in turn agree, in association with one another, to supply all the commercial requirements of the importing countries so long as prices are lower than the maximum price. When prices reach the maximum, member exporting countries undertake to supply member importing countries with a definite quantity of wheat based on their average purchases over a recent period of years at a price not greater than the maximum, and importing countries are released from their obligation to make their purchases from member exporting countries.
The agreement also continues to provide for an annual review of the world wheat situation, which has been an important feature of the 1959 agreement. These reviews are carried out in the light of information obtainable in relation to national production, stocks, prices and trade including special transactions under government assistance programs.
In anticipation of a possible wider participation of exporters in the agreement, member importing countries have accepted a commitment to purchase a larger percentage of their commercial requirements from member exporting countries. Of particular importance is the strengthening of safeguards for the commercial marketings of the exporting countries by means of more precise definitions of what constitute commercial and concessional sales. Furthermore, consideration was also given by the conference to the effective utilization of excess supplies of wheat in raising levels of consumption and assisting in general economic and market development in developing countries with low levels of individual income. While it was recognized that programs to this end are provided for by individual governments and on a multilateral basis, it was agreed that the objectives of the agreement should reflect the concern of the conference for the problems of developing countries.
The new agreement represents a significant advance on the present agreement. With all the important sources of wheat covered by the new agreement, importers will enjoy, despite sharp reductions in wheat supplies, a greater assurance that they will be able to purchase their commercial supplies of wheat at equitable and stable prices. At the same time

International Wheat Agreement exporters benefit by reason of the increased price range, the increased obligations of importing countries and the improved safeguards for commercial marketings. I am glad to say that this new agreement carries the unanimous support of the producer advisers who were members of the Canadian delegation throughout the conference, and I am sure it will equally commend itself to all members of the house. The text of the new agreement will be submitted for ratification at the present session.
The members of the delegation deserve our thanks for the highly successful conclusion of these negotiations. The chief members of the delegation were J. H. Warren, assistant deputy minister of the Department of Trade and Commerce, C. F. Wilson, consul general for Canada at Chicago and W. C. McNamara, chief commissioner of the Canadian wheat board.
The producer advisers who were in attendance were A. W. Runciman, president, united grain growers, Winnipeg; J. S. Stevens, director, united grain growers, Winnipeg; C. W. Gibbings, president, Saskatchewan wheat pool, Regina; A. P. Gleave, president, Saskatchewan farmers union; Saskatoon, Gordon L. Harrold, chairman, Alberta wheat pool, Calgary; W. J. Parker, president, Manitoba wheat pool, Winnipeg.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, inasmuch as the terms of the new three year wheat agreement announced by the Minister of Veterans Affairs on behalf of the Minister of Agriculture indicate a rise of 12J cents a bushel in both minimum and maximum prices under the agreement it should, as the minister suggested, commend itself to all sections of the house. However, it must be remembered that the strengthening of the position of those who are exporting wheat has been largely due to the fact that new customers who were not buying wheat when the last agreement was formulated have appeared in the picture. Most of these are communist countries. In addition to that, the new customers have appeared coincidental with a falling off in the volume of crops of wheat in exporting countries in recent years.
The minister made reference to the exchange rate and the lower value of the Canadian dollar at this time vis-a-vis the United States dollar. I am sure that in this respect the farmers, being an important element in our export trade, will have noted that the Minister of Finance through the exchange fund within the last two months spent $309 million to prevent the Canadian dollar from going lower.
The minister made some reference to the possible entry into the agreement of the

U.S.S.R. It was not clear whether that is probable or merely possible. This, of course, would have a bearing in making the international agreement more secure. I join with the minister on behalf of those on this side of the house in commending the very strong delegation that was sent to this conference. It has always been Canada's practice to send a strong delegation to this important conference. Among the names I recognize many who have previously been delegates to international preparatory conferences.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will appreciate the statement the minister has made, and will wish to compliment the department for the leadership it has given in the signing of this new three year international agreement. The increase in price of 12J cents will go some of the way it is necessary to go to bring about equalization with the increased costs that western farmers, who are most interested in this problem, have to meet. It certainly must be gratifying to all Canadians to know that Canada has been able to play a larger part in arriving at an agreement with respect to an international regulated price, and also that some consideration has been given to the development of new grades for our wheat and that something has been accomplished in this field.
We also appreciate the fact that consideration has been given to new markets and that there is a guarantee that wheat will be available at between the maximum and minimum price to new purchasers. In addition, we appreciate the fact that there will be room within the new international wheat agreement to bring in those new countries that are now going into wheat production, and to assure them of an opportunity to establish themselves in the markets so far as the sale of their product is concerned. I think the fact that Canada has made a contribution to the international wheat agreement is a compliment to the farmers and farm organizations as well as to the department which has assisted in this regard.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, March 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. Balcer for third reading of Bill No. C-67, to authorize the construction and operation on behalf of Her Majesty of a line of railway in the province of Quebec between Matane and Ste. Anne des Monts.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE BETWEEN MATANE AND STE. ANNE DES MONTS, QUE.
speechtext:
In
discussing this bill further on third reading, may I say I believe it is obvious that it is the intention of the government to make a grant in regard to construction of this proposed branch railway line, at least to the extent of the capital costs involved, and that it is the plan of the government to engage in the amortization of those capital costs. In addition, it is also obvious that the government fully understands and, indeed, expects to have to dip into the consolidated revenue fund of the nation for many years to come in order to make the operation of this proposed railway service possible.
I noticed that the minister, in what I considered a very weak defence of the government's position attempted to compare this branch line with the ferry service operated by such boats as the William Carson. To me these are two completely unrelated propositions. On the one hand we have established at public expense and, possibly, even at public subsidy, a ferry service connecting important areas of our Canadian nation. This has no resemblance whatever

Canadian National Railways to the building of a 57 mile long branch railway line in one of the oldest areas of settlement in our nation.
The minister also made a very weak effort to compare this branch railway line with the building of the Hudson Bay Railway. That is almost too fantastic to deserve comment. I am sure the minister must be deeply aware of the fact that at the present time the Hudson Bay Railway happens to serve an important national defence need. In addition, that railway was built for the purpose of establishing an outlet to the sea for a fairly large number of Canadian people. It cannot be compared with a railway branch line which, at best, can hope to serve only 100,000 people.

However, I must deeply disagree with the findings of the committee of this house in regard to this bill, because this bill asks for $14 million of the taxpayers' money now and for an unknown amount of money in the future. This represents a sum of between $140 and $200 for every man, woman and child living in this particular area of Canada. I would much prefer to see the government make a gift to each of the families there; for a family of five this would mean a grant in cash of anywhere from $700 to $1000. I would rather have the government do this than build a railway which we know ahead of time is going to be uneconomic, that for the people of this area will serve no useful purpose that has yet been proved, and that in the years to come will mean an additional burden to the Canadian taxpayer. This is a very serious matter.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE BETWEEN MATANE AND STE. ANNE DES MONTS, QUE.
speechtext:
This is a serious matter indeed. We are asked to pay out $14 million of the taxpayer's money at this time and untold amounts in the years to come. This amount of money would build 140 new hundred thousand dollar industries in that community. I ask the sponsors of this bill whether this approach would not be more useful to the people in the area and receive a more favourable response. This bill represents no solution to our transportation problems. Canadian history is littered with examples of political consideration having taken precedence over national interests in the field of transportation. This is the most barefaced case of its kind in the annals of Canadian transportation development.
I believe the committee ought to have given more consideration to the offer of the truckers of the province of Quebec, to the effect that if the transportation costs that now prevail are a handicap to the people there they would be prepared to reduce their rates if the government would grant a subsidy to make a rate reduction possible. I believe this would be much less costly to the taxpayers of Canada than the proposed extension.
The interest alone on $14 million at even a 5 per cent rate-and in recent years this government has occasionally had to pay a higher rate on its borrowings-runs to $700,000 per annum; in other words $7 for every man, woman and child living in the area to be served. I am convinced they would rather receive $7 worth of aid in cash or in some other form.

I notice with regret that it was reported in the committee that the C.N.R. is only going to be the agent of the government. Neither the C.N.R. nor C.P.R. would touch the project with a ten foot pole. I ask the government who is demanding this railway? Only this morning as I entered the building I spoke to a large number of men from the Riviere du Loup area who were marching on parliament hill with placards. These are business and professional men and workers from other occupations who are requesting assistance in the field of transportation for the people residing south of the St. Lawrence river. I do not know all the facts involved, but their proposal appears to have more merit than the proposal now before us.

Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of repeating what I said at the resolution stage about the bill now before the house.
As I said at that time, we are in favour of the act to authorize the construction and operation, on behalf of Her Majesty of a line of railway in the province of Quebec between Matane and Ste. Anne des Monts.
Over the week end, I tried to remember if similar projects had been discussed under the previous administration, where a crown corporation such as this one, the government owned railways, had decided to build a development railroad.
I know that we have built about ten railroads when we were on the other side of the house. The project which may be not similar but comparable to the one under consideration is the one for which the government had agreed to pay a subsidy for the extension of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway. Of course, circumstances are not the same since that railroad belonged to the province. However, there is a parallel in this that both railroads were intended to serve inland mining developments. That part of British Columbia produces all kinds of minerals: iron, copper, zinc, gold and silver. Moreover the provincial government intended to extend the railroad by stages.
I do not know what the intentions of the present government are with respect to the line under discussion. Once it is built up to Ste. Anne des Monts, perhaps the government will decide to extend it to the copper mine in Murdochville or the mine owned by Federal Metal Corporation. These are matters, obviously, which the minister himself ought to decide.
I got up not only to repeat what I have said before and to indicate what attitude the opposition would take, but to point out that, in this as in so many other things, the government is proceeding without any general plan. The government has no general policy for the development of that region.
The whole lower St. Lawrence region and the adjacent areas such as northern New Brunswick are isolated from the home market because of an inadequate transportation system. Until a general plan, designed to bring a satisfactory solution to this problem, has been applied, that vast region will be in difficulties and have a limited economic development.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in moving his amendment the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam made it quite clear and plain to the house that he did not know all the facts involved. Truer words were never spoken, Mr. Speaker. If he is so interested in the development of that part of the country, I suggest to him that rather than taking a trip abroad he would have been better advised to have gone to that region; because, with the mind of an economist that he is supposed to possess, I am sure he would have come back with different ideas.
He has referred to the unknown amounts of money which this railway may cost the government in the future.
Canadian National Railways
In view of the hon. member's economic assessment, I am less perturbed than ever that very soon this railway will be paying for itself. He suggested we should give to the people of that region, not the opportunity of earning their living and participating in the national economy, but rather that we should give gifts to these people who have been forgotten for 427 years, just as we did to the Indians, to try to keep the peace. Well, Mr. Speaker, the people of the Gaspe peninsula will not accept gifts. They only want a means by which they can participate in the national economy and earn a just and honest living.
I have heard the hon. member for Peterborough trying to find a solution to this problem by suggesting the establishment of a development fund. The trouble in this area has always been that there have been no exits from it, so it was too expensive for people to transport their products to the Canadian or United States markets. What is the purpose of establishing a fund if no one can use it, if no one can partake of it? After hearing these two members of the N.D.P., I am sure that if they intend to use these arguments to try to solve the problems of this country they are in for a lot of headaches. The interest which we attach to this bill is not a political one but one of national interest.
May I be allowed, Mr. Speaker, to say a few words only concerning the views expressed by both the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and the hon. member for Laurier in respect to Cacouna. Cacouna is about 100 miles from where this railway will start, that is about 100 miles from Matane. I am sure that any solution of the problem of Cacouna is not going to solve the problem of Matane or of the lower region of the Gaspe peninsula. Moreover, may I remind hon. members that although I am certainly hopeful something can be done for these people, a project is being developed near Riviere du Loup, which is about ten miles from Cacouna.
Before I commence speaking on the amendment, perhaps I should read a few words uttered by the Minister of Transport in the committee:
Among those familiar with the economy of the lower St. Lawrence region there is general agreement that the lack of railway facilities in the peninsula has so far been an obstacle to development of an area that has traditionally been deprived of ready access for markets. The economic future of the lower St. Lawrence region and more specifically of the Gaspe peninsula is, therefore, directly related to the improvement in its means of transportation. The government appreciates this problem and has decided to do something towards its solution.

Canadian National Railways
Farther along in the same report the minister stated:
Mr. Chairman, I will now give you a brief resume of the wider economic assets of the Gaspe north shore area since I feel that, in the long run, it is on the abundance of these assets rather than on the immediately available tonnages of freight waiting to be shipped that the success of this development will ultimately hinge.
Farther along in the same proceedings the hon. member for Peace River is reported as saying:
Mr. Chairman, possibly I might ask this question of Mr. Scott. Leaving out the economics of the situation vis-a-vis the railway itself, as a result of your examination of the situation, as a result of your discussions and conversations with the corporations in this area, and as a result of your economic evaluation, do you feel that the construction of this railway will, over the years, appreciably add to the gross national product?

Yes. Mr. Fisher says, and quite
rightly, that the tonnage figures 1 gave him are quite small; but you must bear in mind that these tonnage figures do not include one ton of ore, concentrates, or anything of that nature, because we feel that is something that must develop after the railway. While we realize they are there, and hope they will soon be developed-and the quicker the better for the operation of the railway-yet the basic traffic is predicated on what we think is realizable now.
The lack of economic development, Mr. Speaker, is not peculiar to this one region about which we are speaking. There is not one province, Mr. Speaker, that does not have a region which is lacking in economic development. I am happy to see this bill reach third reading stage. It would, moreover, be a serious error to arrest the progress of this measure now and, therefore, arrest the steps being taken to put this project into being and accelerate the economic development of this area by linking the area of Mont Louis and Murdochville to Ste. Anne des Monts. This would give the area access to the industrial centres of Canada and the United States.
Railways have often been built on the basis of hypothetical developments rather than actual developments. I could cite the case of the Baraute railway in 1956, Mr. Speaker, in the Abitibi district. However, at that time it was not found appropriate to proceed with the Gaspe railway. Was it because the government of the day did not have faith in this sector of the country? I will not attempt to answer that question.
The royal commission on transportation do refer to the building of new railway lines. They say:
This is not to say that parliament should not, under certain circumstances, authorize construction of lines for development purposes when the immediate revenue cannot be expected to meet all costs. Under these circumstances, the government should be prepared to meet the deficit from public funds and not place the burden on other shippers.
[Mr. Keays.l
We have earlier recommended that the burden of existing uneconomic lines be removed from the shippers.
Moreover, this same commission recommends that we should look at other methods of transportation, such as road and air. The economy of Gaspe peninsula is based on three things, Mr. Speaker, fishing, farming and mining. I am sure no one has ever considered moving the products of these three industries by air from that area. In so far as highways are concerned, it is a well known fact that certain high revenue products can be moved cheaper by truck than by rail. However, when you consider the products of these three primary industries in the Gaspe peninsula, I am sure you will concede it would be uneconomic to move them by road. To sum up, therefore, it would seem that the government should take responsibility for the development of this project.
On Friday last the hon. member for Port Arthur, who I hope will not engage in too much solipsism, did not seem to concede that others may have a fair idea of the economy of these regions. In his speech he stated that neither the hon. member for Gaspe nor the hon. member Matapedia-Matane was worth $7 million each. The expenditures for economic development are not based on one human value but on a large population's desire to contribute further to national development and enhance further their own economic and social welfare. As I said before, Gaspe is not asking for handouts. It simply requests an opportunity to share in the national wealth and acquire the facilities to realize a higher standard by the labours of its people.
I could go on further and refer to the speech made by the hon. member for Port Arthur. I would ask him to take his pencil and do a little figuring. When he speaks of 50,000 cords of pulpwood I am sure he will believe that this would amount to approximately 75,000 tons. When we speak of 85 million feet of lumber I am sure he will realize this would add up to 127,000 tons. When we speak of wood chips that could be shipped out of the area, I am sure he will realize this would amount to 35,000 tons.
Recently, in fact over the week end, I met a local lumberman from the area who had just received an order for 120 carloads of laths. It is true that at the moment there is a tremendous demand for laths, but a year from now if it is not laths it will be some other by-product of the forests. These 120 carloads, added to the remaining tonnage, would give roughly 250,000 tons of outgoing freight from forest products alone. Added to this would be 65,000 to 75,000 tons moving into the area. When I think of the revenue from this, and when I think of the original

investment of $14 million, based not on 7 per cent as the economic adviser of the N.D.P. wishes to suggest but based on a price of 3.5 per cent, then I am sure the forest products alone could justify the expenditure of this capital amount.
The hon. member for Port Arthur referred to the crown lands, and I think a correction should be made as it is possible that he misunderstood the statement made in the committee. The crown lands of the Gaspe peninsula on the south side of the peninsula, where there is already a railroad are available to all operators. I should say that on the north side of the peninsula the crown lands are there for the use of the lumbermen in the area, and on the south shore most of the land is taken up by large operators and the pulp and paper industry. Therefore there is no problem whatsoever in assuring hon. members of this house that the timber limits are available there to those who wish to use them.
I shall now deal with some of the reasons why shipments of lumber should not all go by water. Not too many regions of Canada and the United States enjoy a water frontage, and although a certain amount of the lumber from the peninsula goes to Montreal, there are in fact only two lumber buyers in that city who can use water facilities so that they may deposit this wood in their yards. Otherwise the lumber must be disembarked from ships and trucked to yards in the interior of the island of Montreal. A large quantity of the lumber produced in this area goes to the United States market but unfortunately there, as well as in the Montreal market, it is impossible to compete favourably with other sections of the country, especially when one realizes that to ship 1,000 feet of lumber from Ste. Anne des Monts to Matane requires an initial cost of roughly $5. That is why these people cannot put their product on the market at competitive prices; it is because of this additional $5 freight charge.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I hope the hon. member for Port Arthur now understands clearly why there has to be other means of transportation than by water for the movement of these forestry products.

In fact, that railway has been asked for, for about a century, as was pointed out the other day by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. English), when he quoted an article from La Minerve, dating back to around 1881.
If, after confederation, we had adopted such a rigid attitude about railway building as we do today in regard to the building of this railway in the Gaspe peninsula, I doubt very much whether railways would have been built in other areas of this country.
The province of Quebec is in need of heavy industry. The lack of railways in the province is said to be one of the main reasons for this scarcity of heavy industry.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker I was interested in the remarks of the previous speaker in relation to this amendment. I think the amendment is an exceptionally good one. The hon. member


who just resumed his seat pointed to the New Democrats and said that perhaps we should be for progress in this particular matter. I would remind him that the Americans have a saying, "Remember Pearl Harbour", and we have one in our part of the country, "Remember Murdochville". I think many hon. members are forgetting one very simple fact, that the Union Nationale is no longer a major force; it is now a very small minority.
We have heard a number of people who have come here and disagreed entirely with the suggestion that this railway should be built. They have made other suggestions. Then we looked at it as an outsider. I admit that I do not know too much about the Gaspe area, but if one looks at a map he will find that here is a stretch of railway that does not belong to the Canadian National Railways. This is privately owned; it is owned by the Canada and Gulf Railway Terminal, whoever they may be. When it is being discussed, usually the man's name that comes to mind is Mr. Jules Brillant. He is the man who controls most of the sea shipping, railways, airways, telephone system, power system and communications system, including radio, press and parts of the television system.
I would therefore suggest that a very small minority of the people are interested in the development that is being suggested to us, and I think we have an obligation not only to the people to see that they get as much as they can for their money, but we must also take into consideration another very important factor in our economy today. I refer to the railway workers.
Over the week end I had the opportunity to talk to quite a number of them who were violently opposed to any railway which is not going to make money, which will have no chance of making money and which is going to be defunct before it ever begins being built under government auspices. They pointed out that labour is always blamed for asking for wage increases. For years the government has been asking to build railways that everybody has admitted could not in the foreseeable future be economic projects. The reason for this railway not being an economic project will be blamed upon the workers and increased wages.
There have been many such railways built and the royal commission on transportation decided many years ago that we had too many railways in the country, particularly branch line railways, many of which are better situated than this railway. The royal commission felt these branch line railways were causing a drain on the economy of the country and they felt that if eliminated it

would enable the central railway system to carry its own weight, or come closer to doing so.
Is this not a problem with which we have been faced for many years? I have no quarrel with those who support the Union Nationale to bring this matter forward. It is true, as the hon. member for Gaspe said, that this railway would have been a wonderful thing 100 years ago. However, it may not be a good thing now. Perhaps they wanted it for 100 years but they have become kind of lost in fact that other methods of transportation may have eliminated to some extent the system that is now proposed.
I think we would be less than honest in this parliament if we were to pass this bill today and not be assured by the government about what is going to happen to the independent railway. There is 50 miles of railway that is to be controlled by the Canadian National Railways or this extension cannot be built. What is the point of putting the tail about 10 feet from the dog? That is not very logical. I suggest that only the government can give us this assurance, and six months is probably the time necessary to make all the arrangements with the owners of this private railway. An arrangement has to be arrived at before the railway is started, and I would think it has to be arrived at before we can even consider how much the railway is going to cost. I would think you have to take into consideration the possibility of expropriation and the ownership of the section that we are going to add to the other 45 or 50 miles of railway that is already in existence and is the connecting link between the Canadian National Railways set up and the rest of the Gaspe peninsula. I think this is an essential. I would think the people of Gaspe would demand that this were done before we made this contribution. I would like to make it very clear that if these considerations are met, I have no objection to the railway being built.
We have listened to the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine stating the resources that are going to be available and referring to the other assets of this railway. He referred to the possibility of the railway obtaining this large tonnage that he outlined. However, I am sure he will agree with me that we in this country are not one bit interested in supplying a transportation system that is not connecting and has no connection with the other railways under the control of Canadian National Railways. It would be quite possible for Mr. Jules Brillant to arrange it so that he were the only person in the area to obtain very much benefit out of this, because negotiations will have to take place with the Canada and Gulf Terminal Com-
Division
pany before the railway operates at all. I believe that for this reason it is absolutely essential that this type of agreement be arrived at. I do not think it is good enough to say that perhaps the possibilities will develop. Perhaps this agreement can be worked out; perhaps it will not be necessary to expropriate the Canada and Gulf Terminal Railway, and perhaps this is good enough.
It may be that this is good enough, but for me it is not good enough, and for the Canadian people it is not good enough. We are not going to buy a pig in a poke. We want to be assured that this railway will be in continuous operation-that it is coming from somewhere and going some place, not just attached to somebody's private railway for a reason which is not particularly clear to me.
On these grounds I think the house might well express its opinion in a straightforward manner by supporting the amendment which is before us so that the committee might have another opportunity to examine the situation and give consideration to the views of other businessmen and interested persons, some of whom we had the opportunity of meeting this morning. These include people who believe that the expenditure of the $14 million is not in the best interests of the people of the Gaspe peninsula and that it will not necessarily bring a sizeable return to those who live in that area.
I think the government would be wise not to compare this proposition with another railway line which has nothing to do with the situation. I think the spokesmen for the government should stick strictly to the point. In addition, I think any such venture as this should be brought within the schedule of the Canadian National Railway Company. I do not see grounds upon which the minister can set up a separate company which would report to the house as an individual entity having no connection with the other railways of Canada. I do not see how the minister can bring forward a proposal of this kind and expect support either from hon. members or from the public of Canada. For all these reasons I believe the house should support the amendment which is before us at the present time.

speakeroldname: Mr. Harold E. Winch (Vancouver East) moved:
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS CONTINENTAL SHELF DISPUTE  SUGGESTED METHOD OF SETTLEMENT
speechtext:
Be it resolved that the House of Commons notes the important issues of responsibility and jurisdiction over the issuance of leases, collection of royalties and control of the continental shelf, being the seaward borders of various provinces and the northern territories, and further recognizes that a federal-provincial dispute has already arisen in connection thereto as both federal and coastal provincial authorities claim sovereignty.
It is therefore recommended, as the opinion of this house, that the government take under advisement a settlement of the dispute in the following manner:	(1) that the issue of sovereignty over
the continental shelf shall be a matter of immediate negotiations between the parties concerned and; that failing an early agreement the matter shall be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada, with an understanding that its decision shall be implemented by the introduction of required legislation and/or an amendment to the British North America Act.
(2)	That as the continental shelf issue Involves the federal government and several provincial governments, that in the interim period pending settlement, agreement be reached that the federal authority issue exploratory leases.
(3)	That all receipts from leases or royalties shall be held in escrow pending a decision on sovereignty either by dominion-provincial agreement or decision of the Supreme Court.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the matter of the continental shelf is one of serious, major and fundamental importance to all of Canada. I am sorry that I found it necessary to put forward such a lengthy resolution, but the question of the continental shelf is so difficult, so complex, so constitutional and so legalistic that I found that the only way by which I could present some of the more serious aspects of the problem and some proposals as to how to resolve the problem for consideration was by drafting the resolution as it now appears on the order paper. In view of the shortness of the time allowed each member in this debate, I am going to endeavour to keep my remarks comparatively brief and with the permission of hon. members I am going to follow very closely some notes I have prepared on the matter.
May I introduce the subject by saying that the seaward borders of the lands of the earth have been under discussion, dispute, exploration and exploitation in recent years. This is happening after nearly 400 years of comparative quiet and stability. However, in the

past few years a multitude of new problems have arisen, problems which are plaguing and have plagued many nations throughout the world and our own country as well.
I am sure that anyone who has followed the subject of the continental shelf will agree that it is obvious now that the same kind of federal-provincial dispute has arisen in Canada over the offshore mineral rights as has given rise to bitter controversy in the United States in the past 20 years. It should be noted, Mr. Speaker, that quite a few months ago the federal authorities in Ottawa issued exploration leases with respect to the continental shelf off the foreshore of the province of British Columbia and a few months after the federal government had issued these leases covering many hundreds of thousands of acres of the continental shelf the government of British Columbia threw down the gauntlet, shall I say, accepted the challenge and issued exploratory leases which in many cases overlap and serve the identical purpose of the leases issued by the federal authorities.
I am going to refer particularly to my own province of British Columbia because it is involved in a dispute with the federal authorities over the questions of sovereignty, the right to issue leases, royalties, control, everything having to do with matters pertaining to the continental shelf. Because this situation is now to the fore in Canada I think it is important to note what has been taking place in the United States.
There have been three important decisions by the United States supreme court holding in essence that the national or federal government, not the states, is possessed of paramount rights in and sovereignty and control over the continental shelf. However, because of the complexity of the agreements, relationships and treaties between various states in the United States and the federal government in that country all these matters have been held in abeyance as a result of the submerged lands act of that country of May 22, 1953.
It is very interesting to note that because the dispute in that country is still unresolved after 20 years and because there are many more cases involved, over $400 million of exploration money is being held in escrow by the federal government until the constitutional issue of sovereignty and control is resolved in that country. Although our constitutional set-up is somewhat different, without a doubt we are facing a similar problem and in some ways it is a larger problem because I do not think it is generally recognized that Canada has a greater continental shelf area than the United States, even if
Continental Shelf Dispute Hudson bay is excluded. In Canada we have a greater area of continental shelf and it is estimated that, with the discoveries of science and new technology, in the future it is going to be worth countless billions of dollars in natural resources and in turn royalties. That is why the question of sovereignty is of such importance to our country.
So far as I have been able to ascertain from all the reading I have done on the subject, the United Nations conference on the law of the sea, which met in Geneva in 1958 with representatives of some 86 countries present, made the first real attempt to establish some international understanding with regard to the continental shelf. It was decided at that conference on the continental shelf by a vote of 57 to three with only eight countries abstaining that the federal authority had sovereignty and control over the continental shelf. Although that was the viewpoint expressed internationally, to my knowledge nothing has been done in Canada to resolve the situation. As a matter of fact, in my opinion the situation is not only ludicrous but absolutely ridiculous. Here we have the federal government issuing leases granting exploration rights on the continental shelf in the territorial waters off British Columbia. Then, we have the province issuing leases covering exactly the same area to do exactly the same thing. What has been the result? The result has been that there is charge and countercharge, insult and counter-insult and abuse. The big companies will not proceed with the exploratory work; they are not moving at all. Why is this so? It is the result of the jurisdictional confusion about sovereignty, as to who has rights, who has control. They do not want to move ahead and perhaps spend millions of dollars, and then find themselves involved in lawsuits or intergovernmental disputes. I say, Mr. Speaker, that it is not in the interests of Canada to allow this condition to continue.
Surely, we do not want to have in our country a repetition of the 20-year battle that has taken place in the United States in the courts with the result that that country as well is being held up in attempts at exploration of the mineral and organic material on the continental shelf which, of course, borders every state and every province that has a waterway or an ocean adjacent to it.
Now, it would be unfair for me to raise the problem and at least not have some idea as to how I think it might be approached. I will admit it is most difficult. Perhaps what I suggest is not feasible, but I have included in the resolution at least my ideas of how the problem may be approached. You will find in the latter part of the resolution under 1, 2 and 3, procedures which I hope will be

Continental Shelf Dispute considered and which it might be possible to have followed. If the procedures set forth therein are not feasible, then at least let us have some kind of constructive action taken. For heaven's sake let us regard ourselves not as a sovereign state in Ottawa, a sovereign state in British Columbia or in Nova Scotia, but as Canadians. Instead of making charge and countercharge, let us sit down as though we were a united nation and try to solve our difficulties. Let us see how we are going to proceed in the interest of Canada.
It is my suggestion that an immediate endeavour be made to bring the federal government and the provinces concerned together to see if an agreement can be reached on sovereignty and on the leases. If that cannot be done, then we should not just let the matter drift. It is my understanding that the government has certain powers. I would say, refer the matter to the Supreme Court of Canada which is the highest body to which we can appeal because no provision is made for the granting of these leases under the British North America Act or other legislation. Let the court tell us what is the proper position to take. After that, let us proceed with this development by agreement, as Canadians, whether it is the provincial or federal government that has jurisdiction. Let us proceed by mutual agreement to introduce legislative amendments or changes in the constitution that would take care of the situation which, of course, was not one which was recognized at the time the terms of confederation were laid down.
However, all that takes time. Why should we wait? I suggest also that there should be an understanding, which I hope can be arrived at, so that we can proceed now, by means of which those who hold leases in British Columbia could proceed with their explorations. If, as I hope, in the not too distant future there is development, then it could be agreed that, until this problem is cleared away and all the disputes resolved, the federal government would issue the leases and hold the moneys received in escrow, the same as they are doing now in the United States. Then, whatever money is there will be distributed on the basis of this new clarification of natural resources power in our country.
This is a subject in which I am keenly interested. I could speak on it at length. I do hope that with these words I have at least outlined the problem and I hope members recognize how serious it is. I believe the suggestions I have made may lay some of the groundwork for a discussion as to how, in the interest of Canada, the potentials of our continental shelf may be developed so that our country can expand. I hope we can solve

this problem in a manner that will qualify us as sensible human beings and members of parliament.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I want to compliment the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) for introducing this resolution. This is an issue that is of extreme importance, particularly in British Columbia. As the hon. member has pointed out to you, the possibility of oil exploration and the hoped for oil development in British Columbia has been slowed because of the failure to establish sovereignty over the resources of the continental shelf. I should like to quote from a publication called Oil-week, of October 9, 1961. This article carries the headline, "Calm Settles Over B.C. Offshore Acreage", and states:
Having made their initial grab of oil rights off British Columbia's coast line, exploration companies now appear content to sit back and wait to see if they filed for permits with the right government.
Even those who played safe and took out permits from both federal and provincial agencies are in no hurry to commence exploration.
Perhaps the companies are not in any hurry, but I think the people of British Columbia are most anxious that this exploration be expedited. For that reason, I can lend a good deal of support to this resolution. Now, the issue of the ownership of minerals, coal and other fossil fuels in the continental shelf extending from our shores is one that cannot be dismissed as unimportant. This is particularly so in British Columbia. There is something in the nature of 15,000 miles of shore line in British Columbia. Of course, this takes in a lot of the islands lying off the shores of British Columbia. We have thousands of miles of inlets or fjords, as some call them. We have a narrow stretch of water between Vancouver island and the mainland. Anyone who cares to take a look at the map of the coast of British Columbia will readily see that this is an extremely difficult problem along that coast.
In my opinion, the problem cannot be dismissed by stating that under the provisions of the British North America Act these rights are vested in the federal government because I have not found that is so. I do not believe it is necessarily so. One cannot say that the settlement of similar disputes in other areas of the world has set a precedent that applies in the case of our own continental shelf area. There is a difference between our constitution and the constitution of the United States, and any settlement that might be made concerning rights in the gulf of Mexico would not necessarily set a precedent for a settlement of a Canadian problem. There have been in the past some contradictions on the part of the federal government that do not bear out the

contention that the continental shelf regions are under the jurisdiction of the federal authority.
I believe it was in 1928 that the provincial government of British Columbia granted oil exploration rights in Hecate straits, lying between the British Columbia mainland and the Queen Charlotte islands. There was a very minor amount of exploratory work done at that time, but as the result of information gained then and as a result of further geological knowledge the oil companies have now taken a new interest in that particular area as well as in others around the coast. For a number of years they have been drilling test holes along the southern part of the Queen Charlotte islands, and have apparently come to the conclusion that the area extending under the sea from the Queen Charlotte islands holds a potential for the discovery of petroleum products.
About two years ago the former minister of northern affairs and national resoures asked me why the oil companies would be applying for exploration rights off the coast of the Queen Charlotte islands. He asked how could they possibly drill in that area. I pointed out to him that a very large part of Hecate straits is comparatively shallow. There is an area extending out some 20 miles which has a water depth of probably less than three fathoms, and after the experience in the gulf of Mexico such a depth of water poses a very minor problem for drilling and exploratory work done in connection with oil.
Now, as I said, there had been some contradictions in the past. I know I am not telling secrets when I say it has been a well known fact that coal operations have been carried out on the continental shelf in the maritimes for many years. I never heard any issue raised over that type of mine there, but I can foresee lots of complications if the federal government insist that continental shelf resources belong to them. In the case of the whole gulf of St. Lawrence and the lower St. Lawrence area, who has the rights to the resources? Who has the rights to the resources in the bay of Fundy?
The federal government does not dispute the right of Ontario to resources lying under the Canadian section of the great lakes. Somebody might say that is fresh water, but it is a huge inland sea and some comparison can be made. The water area of the great lakes exceeds the total continental shelf area lying off the coast of British Columbia. In fact the Ontario section of lake Huron is as large as the area in the region of the Queen Charlotte islands and Hecate straits in which the oil companies are so anxious to pursue exploration work.
Continental Shelf Dispute
I support the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) that the issue , of sovereignty over the continental shelf "shall be a matter of immediate negotiation between the parties concerned". I do not see any reason to expect failure of these negotiations so far as those in British Columbia are concerned. I, as a British Columbian, feel that the mineral and fossil fuel resources of our continental shelf are rightly ours. If a reference is made to the supreme court, as I believe the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources suggested might be done on several occasions, and if the ruling is adverse to the interests of British Columbia, then I feel the law should be amended to redress what I consider is a wrong.
I shall quote again from Oilweek of October 9, 1961, which has a reference to the former minister of northern affairs and national resources, who is now Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton), and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) appearing before a committee of the other place. It reads:
Present, among others, were the then minister of northern affairs, the Hon. F. A. G. Hamilton and the minister of the Department of Justice, the Hon. E. Davie Fulton.
Apparently no subsequent discussion has taken place to up-date this debate, during which Mr. Hamilton made these comments in answer to questions:
"We seek no power to take over the land of any province or any area not described as being precisely within our power ... It is not the intention of the government to force anything on any person or any group that is unwilling to accept."
They were discussing a bill before the house at that time. Later, Mr. Fulton is quoted as saying:
The amendment which is now proposed has been drawn in the desire to make it clear that the operation of this act will not extend to the Pacific coast, in which the province of British Columbia is interested; will not extend to the gulf of St. Lawrence, in which the province of Quebec is interested: will not extend to a large portion of the coast of Labrador, in which that province is also interested; and will not extend to the great lakes, in which the province of Ontario is interested.
In other words, it will be confined to the areas where I understand the lands under territorial waters can be agreed now to be lands within the jurisdiction of the government at Ottawa-
Any suggestion that the federal government has considered itself on firm ground on claiming the resources under our continental shelves, particularly adjacent to the provinces, is not justified in view of the statements of these ministers.
I feel that everything possible should be done to expedite oil and gas exploration on the coast of British Columbia, and clauses (2) and (3) of this motion offer what in my opinion is an acceptable method of breaking the present impasse. I hope that the government of British Columbia will accept such

Continental Shelf Dispute a suggestion and will sit down with our federal officials in order to get this whole matter on the road. We have enough contentious issues between our various provinces and the federal government to weaken us as a nation. I say let us settle those we can, and I believe this is one we can settle. We have a great deal of difficulty in settling some others between the federal government and the provincial government of British Columbia, but I think this is one that can be settled without bad feeling.
I want to say further, Mr. Speaker, that I have never been able to find any indication, nor do I believe it was ever the intention when confederation was conceived, that federal revenues should be drawn directly from the control of natural resources, and I say once again that in my view these natural resources lying off the coast of the provinces belong to the provinces. For the federal government to attempt to draw revenues from these resources might well be classed as nothing but greed and will certainly not encourage the development of our continental shelf resources.
Having said this, I want to impress upon the house and the ministers concerned with these questions that this is an extremely important matter to us in British Columbia. The discovery of oil or natural gas along the coast of British Columbia would give a tremendous impetus to our economy. At present most of our oil is transported long distances by pipe line and is brought in by ships. This results in a fairly high cost to the consumer.
We have our oil resources in the Peace River and we draw oil from Alberta, but the fact is that for one item alone, furnace oil, where I live we pay 20.6 cents a gallon and I believe it can be purchased for anything from 14 to 16 cents in the city of Montreal; and Montreal certainly draws its oil supplies from far distant countries.
I think this points up, Mr. Speaker, the urgent need for a settlement of this continental shelf resources issue and I hope that these oil companies will be able to proceed with their exploration work and a settlement will be reached at the earliest possible date.

speechtext:
I thought I said that I complimented the hon. member from Vancouver East, the same as my colleague from Comox-Alberni. I do not think there is any relationship between a continental shelf and such areas as the great lakes; these are simply depressions inside a continent. The continental shelf is the shallow area which stretches out into the ocean.
It seems to me that we could well have a condition of superior and inferior provinces in this connection. For instance, the provinces which joined confederation in 1867, and British Columbia which joined a little later, were crown colonies which came into confederation bringing with them certain rights guaranteed under the British North America Act. It is quite conceivable that if new provinces are set up in the Northwest Territories this parliament could, in its wisdom, take away from those new provinces any rights to any mineral wealth underneath the continental shelf in the Arctic ocean. We would perhaps then have the older provinces of Canada having certain rights which newer provinces might not have.
There is also the fact that the federal government is in charge of shipping and the fisheries, and it seems to me that by intent the federal government is supposed to look after those matters which are outside the actual land boundaries of the various provinces. I think it would be rather unfortunate if in continental shelf exploration we had varying laws and regulations enunciated by each province which happened to be concerned.
I think one of the factors which has caused the very intensive development in the Northwest Territories has been the fact that we have uniformity in our regulations and we have regulations which were designed for the benefit of Canada, because it is considered that these resources in the Northwest Territories at this particular time must be used for the benefit of all of Canada.
I do think there is a certain precedent in regard to the law of the sea. We do have our own constitution, but in these matters I think that any court of law would take into account the generally accepted international legal procedure, and this must have some bearing upon any decision that is handed down.

However, I think that the hon. member for Vancouver East has got himself into a little bit of a jackbox when he says in paragraph (1):
-implemented by the introduction of required legislation and/or an amendment to the British North America Act.
It is my understanding that the British North America Act can only be amended by unanimous agreement among all provinces. In fact this is one of the weaknesses of our constitution, that if any one province disagrees with something the other nine provinces want to see the federal government go ahead with, the federal government's hands are tied. It could well be that if we must have an amendment to the British North America Act we could never come to any sort of agreement. It would seem to me that if this question were referred to the Supreme Court of Canada, any decision of the supreme court must necessarily become binding on all parties.
I do not think the reference to coal mines being extended out from land areas in Nova Scotia underneath the sea is pertinent to this particular subject, because that resulted from a land development extending into the sea whereas the oil exploration envisaged on the continental shelf is from mobile rigs operating out on the water, in many cases scores of miles from land. We could have a balkanization of Canada; we could have various jurisdictions. This could result in the least advantageous development of our natural resources as far as those resources under the continental shelf are concerned.
It does seem to me that the proposals put forward in this resolution have merit. However, this is an extremely tricky legal problem. It is a problem upon which I think lawyers could spend quite a long time. Lawyers are very interested in the fine points of meaning of clauses and words. This resolution has been developed, I assume, by the hon. member for Vancouver East, who has many admirable characteristics but I do not think he is a lawyer. Neither am I nor the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, and therefore I think this matter would have to be looked at very, very carefully before this parliament committed itself to advising the government that this is the right kind of action. I think the ideas are right and the philosophy behind the resolution is right, but I do not know whether this is the only approach. I think this is a problem for the legal brains of the government to sort of dig into very, very thoroughly.
In regard to agreement and immediate negotiations among the provinces, of course, these can be started at any time, but in order
Continental Shelf Dispute to have negotiation you must have a willingness on both sides to negotiate. It may well be that this will come about; I certainly hope it will. However, knowing the conflict of interests which exists between the various provinces and the federal government, I am not sure. I wonder if it will be as easy as the hon. member for Vancouver East thinks it will.
To sum up, I would say that this resolution should be studied by the appropriate officials in the Department of Justice and by the departments of government concerned. They should understand that this is a problem which cannot be carried forward year after year without anything being done about it. They should realize that it is necessary to reach some sort of conclusion, and if these negotiations do not result in an agreement then the only solution which I can see is the one which the hon. member has suggested, namely to take the matter to the Supreme Court of Canada.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS CONTINENTAL SHELF DISPUTE  SUGGESTED METHOD OF SETTLEMENT
speechtext:
It is not possible for any hon. member from British Columbia to argue against the spirit or the intent of the motion which the hon. member for Vancouver East has submitted. All of us, regardless of party affiliation, are aware that the people of British Columbia require and demand the settlement of the dispute which now exists between the federal government and the provincial government in this matter of jurisdiction over the continental shelf with respect to such matters as the collection of royalties, leases and so on.
As the hon. member for Vancouver East has pointed out, and as other members from British Columbia have indicated, this question of jurisdiction is one of extreme complexity. If one reads the various opinions which have been expressed since this dispute arose it is impossible not to realize that there are many points of view, both legal and otherwise. Even in the oil industry itself there is doubt where the responsibility lies. Further, as the resolution itself suggests, while the major dispute at this moment exists between the dominion government and the government of British Columbia, it is quite possible that any decision or agreement reached by those two authorities would have an impact on the other provinces, provinces which now have an agreed position in relation to their offshore rights on the continental shelf. The position of these provinces might be altered in any understanding or new agreement entered into between the government of British Columbia and the federal government. I do not feel, therefore, that a resolution as all-embracing as this one could be made to work at this stage.

Continental Shelf Dispute
In addition there appears to me to be a possibility that the second and third recommendations in the resolution contain the seeds of a further dispute which might be imposed on the existing one. As hon. members know, agreements between British Columbia and the dominion government have been entered into over many years. There is, for example, the six harbour agreement of 1924 which happened to provide British Columbia with a considerable part of its claim to jurisdiction over the shelf off the coast. But there is no common understanding as to what exactly that agreement provided. There are two interpretations. And so it goes. Throughout this whole discussion we find that the dispute is based on differing interpretations of existing legislation and agreements.
In the first instance, before consideration is given to bringing this matter before the courts, I think that in the interests of both the federal government and the province there should be a meeting between representatives of the departments directly concerned with this matter on both sides to find out if there is some common ground upon which the dispute might be resolved by negotiation outside the courts. At the present time discussions are being carried on at much too long a range. There does not seem to be any great desire on either side to enter upon negotiations in a spirit of conciliation, recognizing that the best interests of the people of British Columbia and, therefore, of the people of Canada, are not being served so long as this dispute continues unresolved. I believe it is necessary that the two governments should try to find some means of gathering together their experts from departments which have a particular interest in this question in an attempt to discover, in conference, whether there is not some ground for common understanding which could provide a basis upon which to proceed. I think that is the first requirement, and surely it is a reasonable one.
My next point is this: there is a good deal of danger that the relationship between the federal government and the government of British Columbia may become, in the public mind both inside and outside British Columbia, something like that which exists between India and Kashmir. We are not separate states. British Columbia is not a separate state; it is an integral part of confederation. The federal government is not, to the best of my knowledge, at war with the government of British Columbia at the moment, though at certain times one might get an impression that such a state almost existed; there are other disputes. I think it is time now to recognize that this is not a question of maintaining the prestige of either government. It is a question of resolving this dispute

to make certain that the people of British Columbia, and therefore the people of Canada, should get the benefit of a long delayed and most necessary resource development. These attempts to protect prestige so often lead to a curious situation where no interests are served, including the attempt to preserve prestige itself. By the time the dispute has dragged on month after month, the people have become tired of it and there is no prestige left for anyone; there is only acrimony, resentment and, on the part of the people, bewildered boredom.
The issue is clear-it is to obtain resource development; to get the economy of Canada further developed. By developing the economy of British Columbia we do develop the econ-nomy of Canada, despite certain suggestions to the contrary which emanate from the west coast from time to time. However, as I say,
I do think the first requirement is a meeting between the representatives of the two governments where the people concerned with resource development and the people who understand the law relating to the situation can meet to decide whether there is not some position which can be mutually agreed or some road which can be followed. It may be that the only agreement which would come out of such a meeting, or series of meetings, would be that the question should be submitted to the supreme court.
If it cannot be done by negotiation then I cannot see any other possible alternative. There would have to be an agreement that when the supreme court decision is made it will be binding on both parties. That is almost entirely what is incorporated in the first recommendation of this resolution.
When you look at paragraphs 2 and 3 of the resolution you realize immediately that the provincial government would have to recognize the federal government's position as a caretaker position in which the federal government would issue exploratory leases during the period of negotiation or while the issue was before the courts and collect the revenues and royalties and hold them in escrow.
I do not think we can go that far in this resolution. I strongly suspect the present temper of the government of British Columbia to be such that it would not be willing to accept the suggestion that the federal government at this time should have even a caretaker authority over the shelf. But of course we cannot really know what the attitude will be unless a meeting is held at which representatives could meet and determine whether they could come to an agreement on points such as those raised by the resolution now before us, and on others

which may exist. While there is no agreement at the moment and no meeting of minds between the federal and provincial governments there is certainly not merely a hiatus in the consideration of this question. The issue is a live one here in Ottawa in the departments of the federal government concerned, as well as in British Columbia. The positions of the two governments and their arguments to support those positions must be clearly defined and established. Consequently it is time now to bring about a means by which a conference can be held. I would hope that from the conference would emerge the means by which there can be achieved settlement of the question whether merely by negotiation or by reference to the supreme court.
As to the points contained in paragraphs 2 and 3, they will perhaps come up. As a matter of fact I suppose those two points cannot be avoided in any negotiations; but I do not think the federal government should be bound to include them at this stage in view of the fact that there may be other approaches the federal government has assessed and is prepared to introduce in the negotiations, if they could be reopened.
I return to my original contention that it is impossible for a member of this house from British Columbia to oppose the spirit and intent of this resolution, but the only part of the resolution which strikes me as being entirely valid at this time is that contained in the first paragraph recommending that a meeting be held to deal with the problem and attempt to find a means of settlement which the people of British Columbia are now demanding be achieved.
