Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate -very briefly, as I see by the clock-I wish to compliment the hon. member for Vancouver East on proposing this resolution, but I wish to state that it involves issues of such magnitude, both legal issues and others, that it can scarcely be discussed in the hour reserved for consideration of private members bills. I do not consider myself a constitutional expert nor do I appreciate all the ramifications of the British North America Act, but it appears to me that there are raised in this resolution matters of great magnitude and of vital importance, not only in relation to the development of Canada but to that of each individual province.
We are dealing here with the continental shelf which in my opinion has never been exactly defined. We do not know how far it goes seaward or where it starts landward.
Supply-Forestry
The maritime provinces, although not to the same extent as British Columbia, are interested in the development of the continental shelf. I believe it was in 1925 that the legislature of the province of Nova Scotia passed an act vesting the foreshore of the province in the provincial government. Nothing was said as to the ownership or rights in the territories beyond, in the land beyond the foreshore. The fact that over the years some of the collieries in Cape Breton have extended their operations out under the sea does not in my opinion establish any claim except possibly that of adverse possession, but certainly not any inherent right of sovereignty.
The province of New Brunswick on the other hand has not passed such an act. We have grants in the province of New Brunswick that came from the imperial government, the government of Great Britain, under which the grantee is given rights to low water mark. A former chief justice of the province of New Brunswick now deceased decided that the province owned the land under the ocean for many miles. Whether or not that decision was correct, I am not prepared to say. In my opinion the first thing that must be decided is what is the extent of the continental shelf.
As hon. members know under the British North America Act certain fields of jurisdiction were assigned to the federal and provincial governments. According to some constitutional experts a residual power is also vested in the federal government under which anything not assigned to the jurisdiction of the provincial governments is vested in the federal government altogether apart from the section dealing with peace, order and good government. It may be that as the continental shelf is not mentioned as coming within the jurisdiction of the provincial government, it remains vested in the federal government.

Mr. Chairman, I think we last dealt with this item on February 23. Before that time and since, I have had the opportunity of having a couple of conversations with the minister in connection with wood preserving. On behalf of the new industry in my riding, as well as four others which I believe were started elsewhere in Canada in 1961 and two additional ones which are expected in 1962, I have been suggesting to the minister that the forest products laboratory should endeavour to work in closer conjunction with the spending departments such as transport, public works and those other government departments which are perhaps the biggest purchasers of preserved wood in Canada.
I am speaking, of course, of a relatively new process so far as Canada is concerned, the waterborne preservative known as the Boliden salt process, whereas most of us are more familiar with oil treatments for wood preserving. So far as my riding is concerned, there seems to be quite a scope for the utilization of wood species such as poplar, which we have in great abundance, that are sometimes described as wood weeds. In our area we no longer have, of course, the wonderful white pine that made the early mills in northwestern Ontario so famous, and because of freight rates and so on the import of fir and other more popular products is sometimes prohibitive. The result is that products other than wood are being used in substitution.
I am told that a number of additional plants using this new process could be established if there was not quite so much rigidity in the acceptance of certain standards that have been traditional in this country. Those who have spoken to me seem to feel that, without adequate initiative and experimentation in Canada, we have been inclined simply to accept United States standards and have been ignoring the fact that while this particular process is new in Canada it has been well known for some time in European countries, particularly the Scandinavian countries. I believe that this particular salt waterborne preservative has been utilized in Europe since 1935.
As I understand the situation, the minister's forest products laboratory is prepared to tell any possible purchaser of wood for which a preservative is required that a standard of .55 with respect to the Boliden salt process is adequate rather than the standard of .65 set by the Canadian standards association. The point I wish to make to the minister is that, first of all, the countries of Europe,
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Chown).]
New Zealand and others have accepted a standard of less than .55 but if in the opinion of our laboratory .55 is satisfactory it seems to me that information should be conveyed properly to such departments as the Department of Public Works, which establishes specifications for the purchase of wood that is required in many of its structures. I urge that the department go beyond that and establish whether a standard of .55 is not higher than necessary and whether there is not undue conservatism in this particular field.
I happened to listen to a farm broadcast on the radio at noon and the subject under discussion was the forest products laboratory and the preservatives that are available for treating farm fence posts and so on. There is a tremendous field here, of course, in so far as the weed woods are concerned and there would be tremendous industrial and economic advantage to our part of the country in the use of this process. I know the same thing is true in Manitoba because I know that a plant of this type has been established in the constituency of the hon. member for Dauphin. At first the plant had a hard time selling the product but now they are working to full capacity. I understand that the governments of Saskatchewan and Manitoba have accepted this preservative with respect to such purchases as telephone poles. Hon. members know, of course, that in those provinces the telephone companies are government owned.
I suspect that there has perhaps been undue reliance on United States standards rather than doing our own experimenting independently. There is a feeling that, in relation to oil treatment preservatives, a standard of lower than .55 could properly be accepted with regard to this process. If this were done it would certainly generate a substantial cash flow that is not available at the present time in areas such as mine and other rural areas, particularly in western Canada, where there is this immense asset in the form of unused poplar wood.

I should like to speak on this item for two reasons, the first being an item that appeared in the newspapers across this country. The article to which I refer appeared in the Globe and Mail for Thursday, March 8, datelined Vancouver, B.C., and reads:
A major expansion of the Elk Falls pulp and paper mill on Vancouver island at a cost of $25 million was announced today by Crown Zellerbach Canada Ltd.
G. H. Gallaway, company president, said the expansion would mark the first production in Canada of bleached kraft pulp from sawdust.
The expansion will add 50,000 tons of sawdust pulp a year; increase the kraft pulp production to 1,000 tons from the present 520 tons a day and triple the Elk Falls bleach plant capacity to 600 tons a day from 200 tons.

The Elk Falls plant, just north of Campbell river, on Vancouver island's east coast, brought into production in 1952, cost $65 million. It is operated by the Elk Falls Company Limited, a division of Crown Zellerbach.
"This is the biggest single expansion our company has undertaken." said Mr. Gallaway. Completion is scheduled for 1964.
I believe, the article was in error in setting the capital cost of this expansion at $25 million because I understand the official press release stated it would be $35 million.
Now, Mr. Chairman, this is a very important breakthrough in applied science. For many years it has been a dream to use sawdust as a raw material in the production of pulp. One often hears private business being castigated for its alleged failure to participate in research work. One also often hears, both in this house and outside, suggestions to the effect that United States industrial firms operate on a basis of cut out and get out in Canada. This development at Elk Falls was made possible because of the wealth of research knowledge the parent company, Crown Zellerbach, has gathered not only through its own research facilities but from all the sources available to it in the United States, Canada and indeed throughout the world. There may be a pulp plant in some other part of the world which is successfully using sawdust as a source of raw material, but I do not know of one. While I take an interest in forestry matters and forest products, I am not aware of another plant that is using sawdust for this purpose.
I should like to point out, Mr. Chairman, what this development means from an economic and forestry point of view, particularly in British Columbia. It is of particular significance to our future economy. This development means that our pulp industry has available to it a low cost raw material that will help make it competitive in other parts of the world and still provide working conditions for the labour employed in pulp mills that are as good as any place in the world. I believe I can safely say that. I believe working conditions in our pulp and paper industry are as good as any in North America, and consequently any place in the world.
In the case of this one plant, our forest products production is increased by the equivalent of 40 million board feet of timber a year without cutting one additional tree. The value in dollars of this pulp I will not attempt to estimate, but it runs into many, many millions of dollars. The annual output of sawdust waste in British Columbia, if it were economically available, would supply the raw material requirements for upwards of 25 such plants as this one proposed at Elk Falls. I said if it were economically possible because
Supply-Forestry
I think that is getting into the realm of fantasy. Many of the saw mills are in remote areas and there would be a real transportation problem in getting the sawdust to the pulp mills. I doubt if, by any stretch of the imagination, the sawdust waste of all saw mills could be used in the pulp mills of British Columbia.
One important fact of this new pulp development is the fact that in British Columbia there is no question about whether timber should be converted into chemical use or sawn into lumber products in saw mills. Both types of plants are an integral part of the over-all forest industry. One is just as important as the other, and a healthy pulp and paper industry needs a healthy lumber industry and the latter needs every possible assistance from research in order to sell its products in competition with materials available from sources other than wood.
This consideration of materials other than wood brings me to a subject that is very much in the mind of anyone who has knowledge of our British Columbia forest industry. I have referred to this before on a number of occasions, and I am speaking of our cedar problem. I feel that a crash research program is needed to find a solution to this problem. About 25 per cent of our coastal stands of timber is western red cedar. This would probably amount to about 100 billion feet board measure of timber. I have not the figures for the interior, but I would estimate that about 10 per cent of the interior stands are western red cedar. They are primarily situated in the Kootenays, the Columbia river valley, the lower Thompson and some of the areas around Salmon Arm and Enderby. There is much of this cedar that is of high quality and produces a high grade product in the form of cedar siding, cedar panelling, shingles, shakes and other products.
We have run into very severe competition in recent years from substitute materials. We are finding it difficult to convert a large quantity of this cedar into sawn products that we can sell. In fact, a few weeks ago, within the last two weeks, I believe, there was an announcement from MacMillan, Bloedel and Powell River Company that they were closing the cedar mill operation at New Westminster. This plant has been known as the B.C. Manufacturing plant, and because of the difficulty in finding markets for the products from that mill, the plant is closing. I believe this factory employs approximately 265 men and it uses approximately 75 million board feet of cedar a year. Where is a market going to be found for these 75 million feet of logs? They are going to come out of the woods because the cedar is interspersed amongst the

Supply-Forestry
other species required for lumber, pulp and paper, and they will be produced whether or not there is a market for them. This is a problem that is increased year by year and I believe it has been brought to the attention of the minister and his officials by the forest industries association for British Columbia. I have a copy of the brief that was presented to the minister about one and a half or two years ago, shortly after he became Minister of Forestry. I should like to quote from this presentation which deals with the particular problem of the British Columbia forest industry and which shows how the Department of Forestry could best aid that industry. It states:
The percentage of cedar In the coastal forest inventory is very high, in fact more than four fifths of the total cedar inventory of North America is in B.C.'s forests. The actual percentage of cedar in our coastal inventory is about 24 per cent, yet, for many years, the percentage of cedar being cut annually is much lower than the percentage of that species in the total forest inventory, the percentage of cedar being cut being only about 17 per cent. This percentage has represented the maximum volume that existing or known commercial uses have been able to absorb. As a consequence of the low percentage being cut, the western cedar problem each year becomes more serious. A very high percentage of this cedar (which is known as "western red cedar") is suitable only for shingles and low grade lumber, for which there is a limited demand.
As a result of the combination of circumstances referred to in the preceding paragraph, you will appreciate that the utilization of cedar is one of our industry's most serious problems. Leading forest engineers and chemists, who have studied the problem are convinced that the only real solution to the problem of using low grade red cedar is partly in increased use in the manufacture of pulp but chiefly in finding, through research, a wider range of commercial uses for cedar, including chemical extractions thereof.
I should like to emphasize the importance of this problem to the minister and stress what it means to the economy of British Columbia. It is what I might refer to as one of the soft spots in our economy and I feel that most people who have a knowledge of the B.C. forest industry-I think I have some knowledge of it myself-believe that with a concentration on the part of the Department of Forestry, with its facilities for research, there is every reason to be confident that the department would come up with the anwer to this problem. I ask the minister to give it his personal attention at the earliest possible date.

This is the first time I have had the opportunity to take part in discussions on the estimates of the new Department of Forestry, and it is a department which I believe will reach considerable prominence in service to Canadians in the future. The minister brings to his post a very wide and practical knowledge of the forests

of Canada in general, and of the forests of his own province of New Brunswick in particular. Through you, Mr. Chairman, may I say to him that I wish him well in his efforts.
During my years in this house I have always been particularly interested in matters pertaining to research. I have enjoyed many of the meetings of the House of Commons committee on research, of which I am a member, but to date we have not been able to get to the point of discussing research in forestry. I hope that some time in the near future we shall be able to do that.
I believe Canadians are becoming more aware of the value and the need for research. However, I think that over the years we have not had sufficient research in Canada, and viewing the estimates of expenditures by other countries on research I would say that we have allocated a smaller proportion of our gross national product to research than many other countries in the western world. We in this country have a great and varied storehouse of natural resources. In fact I believe it is fair to say there are few countries in the world in a better position to carve a great economic prosperity through research and technology than Canada. To no small degree our economic stature in the future will depend on the nature and degree of our research, and the manner in which research findings are utilized. I would point out that these general observations on research would apply not only to forestry but also to many other industries.
The industries and the national economies which put a premium on research will do the best in the years that lie ahead.
Dr. E. W. R. Steacie, president of the national research council, when speaking at the opening of the addition to the Imperial Oil research laboratories at Sarnia in January of this year said:
Any industrialized country that does not allocate to research a proportion of its national effort comparable to that of the most advanced nations will be unable to maintain its position in the world.
Later in his speech, when referring to the rate of growth of organized scientific activity, Dr. Steacie said:
As yet, however, there is no sign that the rate has started to decline, and one must conclude that any country which does not increase its expenditures on research at a comparable rate will ultimately face a deterioration in its world position.
This item for a further amount of $80,000 for forestry research is one with which I can agree. In a country where research needs increased attention, both on the part of government as well as industry, it is good to see a lead being taken by the federal government. We must have a greater emphasis on research and an increase in desirable jobs. Otherwise

this country will lose some of its best trained people. In this connection I would point out that in 1959, of the 90 science-trained doctors of philosophy who left the national research council, only 16 remained in Canada.
Research is not only for industries which are not as successful as they might be. It is also essential for industries that are successful today and hope to maintain their competitive position for tomorrow. In no case is this truer than in that of the forest industries.
There is no need to comment on the value of forest industries to the Canadian economy. In the newsprint industry alone 127 pulp, paper and paperboard mills across the country not only provide 47 per cent of the newsprint supply of the free world and account for 4.3 per cent of our gross national product, but they furnish the basic materials for almost another 450 mills providing employment for our people.
The importance of this industry to the economy of Canada was well expressed in a speech made last March by the minister to the Canadian forestry association in which he said that the aid which he expected his department to give to the forestry industry would include research relating to the utilization of forest products. Then he went on to say this:
"The public must be awakened", said Mr. Flemming, "to the realization that the forest resource is Canada's vital concern, without which the standard of living would be very drastically depressed, and without which the whole economy might well crumble".
The basis for the forest industries in
Canada-as of course it is everywhere else______
is the raw material which our forests are able to provide. Much research will be necessary if we are to ensure adequate supplies of present plant capacity and also for increased capacity in the future. This is true for Canada in general and I think it is particularly true for other regions of Canada, particularly the Atlantic provinces.
It has been estimated that the forest industries of Canada can provide another 125,000 jobs. To do this there will be need of research. There will be need of research to appraise our present capacity and how it can be used to meet future needs. There will be need of research to develop the most effective and efficient use of wood. Research will be needed to provide new and improved methods of protecting our forests from the ravages of fire, insects and disease. Again, research will be needed to acquire more knowledge and positive information regarding tree genetics, tree improvements and artificial tree generation.
In the Atlantic provinces there are 80 million acres of forest land, most of which is accessible. This is a tremendous benefit to the 26207-1-109
Supply-Forestry
Atlantic provinces because the forest industries play a major role in the regional economy. Over 20 per cent of the total production of the Atlantic provinces comes directly from forest industries. In the years ahead the economy of the eastern provinces will rest largely on the expansion of these industries, provided the supply of raw material can be maintained. In my view this will largely depend on the results of research by governments and by the industries concerned.
In my own province of Newfoundland the forest industries, particularly the newsprint industry, form the backbone of the economy of the province. They provide about 25 per cent of the total value of all production. The newsprint industry in Newfoundland is not only vital to the areas in which newsprint plants exist, but also to the whole province. Much research and careful implementation of resulting programs will be needed if wood supplies are to be sufficient for present capacity and proposed new capacity. I believe that only research can give the necessary directed activity.
In recent years there have been research projects to accumulate information necessary to any reforestation program. Tree planting and direct seeding projects have provided invaluable data regarding where reforestation is necessary and where it is likely to succeed. These projects, originating in 1950, have been directed in part to burned-over areas to determine the assistance required in different regions for the forests to reproduce in a satisfactory manner. In view of the abnormally large increase in burned-over areas, particularly in the last year, I would hope that both these projects would be given further consideration and attention.
Mr. Chairman, of particular importance at the present time is the need for research into the insect infested forest areas of Newfoundland. While we do have serious infestation in certain areas by the hemlock looper, the spruce budworm, the balsam fir sawfly and the larch sawfly, it is with the balsam woolly aphid that I would like to deal briefly. Insect surveys are not new to Newfoundland. In 1925 Dr. J. M. Swaine made an inspection trip across the island. It is interesting to note that at that particular time no mention was made of the woolly aphid in Newfoundland.
A few days ago when my hon. friend from Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador was referring to this problem he too was concerned about infestation in the forests in his own area. Reading back over the history of research in Newfoundland I note that although there were some writings by Dr. Swaine in 1925 there were no further reports until 1937 following the Newfoundland insect survey of

Supply-Forestry
1936. I do not have the lull text of that report, but the information I do have leads me to believe that again there was no mention of the woolly aphid in the forests of Newfoundland. The purpose of this survey in 1936 was to get some idea as to where the outbreaks were and to identify the insects responsible. In 1934 Mr. C. C. Loughlin was appointed as the first insect officer, sponsored by Bowater (Newfoundland) Pulp and Paper Mills Ltd. and the Newfoundland forest protection association, an association, incidentally, which in 1960 celebrated its 50th year of commendable forest activity.
Following a survey made in 1949 by officials of the forest biology division at Fredericton, New Brunswick, Mr. W. J. Carroll recommended, in particular, the conducting of a special study of the infestation of the Newfoundland forests by the balsam woolly aphid. While this was the first occasion that this insect had been identified, it would appear that it had been introduced into the southwestern part of Newfoundland by about 1930. In 1955 a forest biology laboratory was constructed at Corner Brook, Newfoundland, and since that time a good deal of useful information has been compiled under the able direction of Mr. Carroll.
Today the woolly aphid poses a serious threat to the health of the Newfoundland forests. The woolly aphid attacks only true firs, but the balsam fir is particularly susceptible to damage. This particular species of tree comprises about 75 per cent of the softwood stands in western Newfoundland and about 60 per cent of those stands in central and eastern Newfoundland.
At the present time infestation on the Burin and Avalon peninsulas is not severe enough to be considered as an immediate threat. This infestation is spreading at an approximate rate of 10 miles per year, which I understand is double the rate in the maritime provinces, with the resulting danger of a spread into the wider areas of central Newfoundland. It is known from surveys that were made last year that there are now about 3,000 square miles of forest land in Newfoundland infested by the woolly aphid. Possibly I can best give the committee an idea of the rapid spread of this insect by quoting from a paper prepared by Mr. W. J. Carroll and presented to the annual meeting of the Canadian institute of forestry held in Corner Brook in November, 1961. The writer states on page four of his paper:
An indication of the rapid development of the Humber valley outbreak is shown in survey plot records from near Steady Brook. The plot is located in an immature stand of balsam fir and is fairly typical of stand conditions in most of the Humber valley. In 1959, 72 per cent of the trees showed no visible injury. In 1960, 5 per cent were uninjured

and in 1961 only 1 per cent. Trees in the moderate to severe damage class changed from 1 per cent in 1960 to 29 per cent in 1961.
This is a problem of increasing seriousness and one which merits the attention of the appropriate department of the provincial government and the pulp and paper companies on the island as well as the lumber companies concerned. I also hope that this program will receive priority in any forestry research undertaken by the federal government.

I should like to associate myself with the remarks made by my hon. friend from Humber-St. George's. He has given an account which is quite clear and I hope the minister will show the interest in this problem that he has already shown with regard to our other difficulties. I remember that last summer when the fires were raging in Newfoundland the minister came to Gander and showed a personal and a knowledgeable interest in our problems there. At that time, as hon. members know, we had lost huge areas of timber through forest fires. The minister has first hand knowledge of these fire-blackened areas; he knows how difficult it is to grow trees again on areas which have been burned over.
Our two great problems at the moment are recurring forest fires and the threat of the woolly aphid. I should like to thank the minister for a copy of the paper entitled Reforestation and Research in Newfoundland. Among other interesting information in this paper is an account of how difficult it is for trees to be grown on areas which have been burnt over. I should like to suggest, if such a suggestion need be made, that research be conducted into the possibility of reseeding or re-afforesting these areas. It is my belief that the adverse effects of these fires will become more apparent within two or three years than they are at the present time, because the absence of this timber, which is the basis of the livelihood of so many people, when fire-killed wood has been cut, will then be felt severely. Here is a problem which I trust the minister and his department will attack with the zeal in research which is necessary if what is apparently, at the present time, a great tragedy is to be averted. The adverse effects on the economy could at least be mitigated if we could find a means of successfully replanting these devastated areas. Research into preventive measures is, I agree, of even greater importance, although a cure is important, too, in view of what happened last year and the destruction which occurred.
In relation to preventive measures, research into the best type of aircraft capable of being used for water bombing is a field of great importance. We should try to determine

whether land-based aircraft or water-based aircraft are most effective for dealing with fires. Actually, research in all its phases is important because we have outgrown what I might call the pioneering attitude toward our forests. Nature was good to Canada; nature was even prodigal in supplying Canada with resources, and I am afraid that in the early days our own attitude toward these resources was prodigal also. But we have reached a point where conservation and the replenishment of our resources is necessary if we are to maintain our supplies of wood products. In these circumstances, money spent on research is well spent.

There are just one or two matters that I would like to bring to the attention of the minister while the committee is dealing with this vote. The first has to do with the compulsory grade marking of lumber. At the present time this is due to come into effect on April 1 of this year. I am in agreement that lumber should be graded and stamped accordingly, but at the present time the only recognized grade marking comes under the control of the interior lumbermen's manufacturing association of British Columbia. Even properly graded lumber is not acceptable to the national housing authority or to the C.M.H.C. if it has not been stamped by a stamp issued by the interior lumbermen's manufacturing association. This process is very expensive for the smaller mills of which there are a great number in British Columbia. They must either join this association or content themselves by selling rough lumber to the larger companies. At the present time there are just not enough men in British Columbia to undertake all this grading work. This is evident from the large number of advertisements appearing in papers throughout the province asking for men with the proper qualifications for this work. I have had considerable correspondence on this matter and I learn that even certain companies are not accepted by the I.L.M.A. They are not recognized and their grade stamping is not recognized. I have heard from one concern, the California lumber inspection service which applied some months ago for recognition by this lumber manufacturers' association, but even after volumes of correspondence and questionnaires they are still waiting for a reply to their request. Therefore, it appears that the interior lumbermen's manufacturing association has a monopoly over the grading of lumber in the province of British Columbia.
A great number of our smaller mills-and we have a large number of smaller mills in the province-are not members of these larger organizations. One reason for this is that it is very expensive to join and the smaller mills working on small tracts of timber are 26207-1-109J
Supply-Forestry
not able to afford to join these larger organizations. It is considerably more costly to obtain the services of one of these companies which perform grade stamping. It does not seem fair that any one association should be able to carry on a monopoly of grade stamping. The smaller organizations feel they should be able to choose how and by whom their lumber will be graded. The situation at present is that the smaller lumber concerns are being forced to join associations of which they do not wish to become members.
I bring this matter to the minister's attention and point out that I recognize that the grading of lumber is an art, but at the same time the grading is only as good as the eye of the man who grades the lumber. Therefore a stamp on the lumber is only as good as the grader who grades it. I feel some consideration should be given at this time to making some arrangements with the smaller concerns so that stamps can be made available to them either through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or the government itself. The government could issue licences and stamps to the smaller mills so they would not be forced to go to the more expensive mills in British Columbia.

Mr. Chairman, in all the observations which have been made there are undoubtedly many useful suggestions and many proper inquiries, so I feel at this time it is fitting that I make some observations in connection with what has been said by various hon. members this evening. If I do not refer specifically to every point that has been raised I urge the various hon. members who raised the points not to be discouraged and not to hesitate to bring my oversight to my attention in a personal way.
I wish first of all to refer to the question raised by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River with respect to the preservative to be used in connection with wood. In order to make a somewhat brief story of what could be rather extended remarks I can assure the hon. gentleman that the Boliden salt process -which I am sure is very well known to you, Mr. Chairman-has received a great deal of attention. It is something that is receiving more and more attention each day. The particular division of the department in charge will take under consideration the comments which have been made by the hon. member. Personally I am not an expert on penetration.
I do not know whether .55 is enough or whether it should be .65 or whether the United States standards should or should not be rigidly adhered to, but I do assure the hon. gentleman that the director of the forest products research branch in the department is an expert in this type of treatment and I assure

Supply-Forestry
the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River that his representations will be brought to the attention of Dr. Jenkins.
I was interested in and I must say very pleased by the remarks made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni because in my opinion, as my hon. friend said, the utilization of sawdust does represent a definite breakthrough so far as up to the minute advance is concerned. The hon. gentleman referred to the utilization of a very large percentage of the total product of the forest as it is represented by what is ordinarily known as sawdust.
In my young days in connection with saw milling, sawdust and the disposal of sawdust were terrible problems. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni mentioned that a $50 million or $60 million extension of an existing plant will come into being which will be based on the use of sawdust as a raw material from which kraft pulp will be made. I think this is a tremendous step, and as the hon. gentleman said it will have the effect of preserving the forest and making us more competitive. I am sure this is extremely important news for the forest industry in general.
I remember very well the question of the use of cedar which was brought to our attention more than a year ago. We were asked to give it concentrated effort and this has been done. If I had been requested to make an observation or guess about which of the two problems was the more difficult to solve- that is, finding an answer to the question of the more extensive use of cedar and finding an answer to the question of what could be done with sawdust-I would have said that the use of sawdust represented the more difficult problem. Yet we find that a plant based on the utilization of sawdust is practically assured at this time. I can only say to the hon. gentleman that efforts will continue so far as the use of cedar is concerned. Perhaps there might be a little more co-operation between the province of British Columbia and private industry and perhaps the research directed toward that specific problem by the department could be intensified. Toward that end I assure my hon. friend that I will cause some more inquiries to be made with a view to seeing whether we can have a little more concentrated effort.
I visited Vancouver within the last year or so and was greatly impressed by the calibre of the men who are working in the forest products laboratories. I am sure they are excelled by none engaged in similar work anywhere in Canada. If we had similar people engaged in this work in the maritimes probably they would be, but we do not have people engaged in work of that nature down

there. In any event I have some understanding of the problem and my hon. friend may be sure we will continue to work toward accomplishing something more specific in connection with it.
I was keenly interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Humber-St. George's in connection with research. We in the maritimes are most interested in research because our trees are not large in size. I believe we have to look to research as a means of achieving more production per acre in the future. I recognize the value of what he has said about the problem of reforestation, to which problem the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador also directed our attention. Since the most disastrous fire of last year this problem has seriously occupied the attention of the department, as hon. gentlemen may have noted by the paper on the subject that has been released. That is a start.
I know something about the newsprint industry and I have some conception of its value to Newfoundland. I am not very conversant with the problems arising from the blight of the woolly aphid that has affected the balsam. I do know it is recognized by those in our department who are charged with that special responsibility as being a particularly difficult situation. Efforts are certainly being made toward improvement in that respect. I was very much impressed, though I must say not very favourably impressed, by the remarks that were made in connection with the steady progress that has been made by this particular pest or insect or call it what you like. I can quite understand the concern of my hon. friends opposite. We cannot promise any miracles because the days of miracles may be pretty well over as far as forests are concerned. Perhaps they are not; in any event, we will hope for the best. But I do assure hon. members that the department and those connected with it are very conscious of the importance of this matter and they are also very conscious of the difficulties in connection with it.
The hon. member for Kootenay East referred to grade marking. I can quite understand his concern in connection with this matter. A day or two ago I was at a luncheon where representatives of the lumber industry from the Atlantic to the Pacific were gathered. There were something like 50 or 60 present. Two of them were from the interior of British Columbia. I believe it was the interior lumbermen's association with headquarters at Penticton that was represented thereby two of the men who are specially charged with the responsibility of exercising some supervision over grade marking.

I mentioned the matter to them and they were both quite satisfied that the situation would be dealt with and would be dealt with in a way that would not cause any particular hardship to small mills. If my hon. friend will discuss the matter with me on some other occasion, we will try to get something a little more specific than that. I do know something about that situation with respect to the province of Newfoundland because, as hon. members perhaps recall, recently the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate raised the point in the house. I find that the government of Newfoundland has been communicated with in order to have some of their staff get in touch with the maritime lumber bureau to obtain the necessary knowledge, even though this does involve a trip to Fredericton or some other place where there are courses in grade marking. The purpose is to train a few of the representatives of the department of forests of the province of Newfoundland so that the inspection service will be readily available and at moderate cost.
I believe that concludes the remarks I wish to make in connection with the observations made by the various hon. members this evening. There will presumably be a time when the forestry estimates will come before the house again and I would expect to make somewhat more extended remarks then concerning our aims, hopes and expectations with regard to future forestry activities on the federal level. Tonight I will content myself with making these perhaps sketchy observations in connection with the points that have been raised, and I assure all hon. members that if it is their wish to pursue them further with me privately I will be very happy to see them at any time.

With respect to the hon. lady's remarks, may I say that the matter does concern Indian training in large part, and since the minister did indicate this afternoon that the matter will be looked into it may well be there is considerable information which is not in her possession and which if given at a later time on the main estimates might not be of as great assistance as it would be now. speechtext:
Order. Perhaps there is a certain responsibility resting on the Chair in connection with this problem. I find on reading the items in the estimates here that they relate to repairs and upkeep of buildings and works, and community employment projects. The difficulty I am going to have is that if I allow the hon. lady to continue discussing the subject she has chosen to introduce on these estimates, I am going to have a problem ruling against other hon. members who might wish to comment on the same subject, perhaps even the hon. member for Skeena to whom she has referred, although he is not in the house at the moment. If he were here, undoubtedly he would want to make a contribution to the debate.
I ask the hon. lady, therefore, to co-operate and see that she does not make my job too difficult, realizing that another opportunity will arise, perhaps more than one opportunity, to discuss this subject. For instance, the first item of the main estimates of the department would be one opportunity, and then orders of the day might be another. I would ask her to co-operate. I will listen very intently to what she has to say and if I can relate it to the item, I shall do so. If other hon. members of the committee do not interrupt, she may proceed.

I should like to speak to the point of order, Mr. Chairman. It is a point which you have raised, yourself, but which the minister has not seen fit to raise. Your Honour has referred to the fact that this matter could be discussed on another occasion, namely during consideration of the main estimates. The point is, and I submit this to you respectfully, that it can be raised under this item now.
The reason I make this statement is that the first item under discussion in these supplementary estimates concerns Indian agencies, operation and maintenance. It would seem to me that the hon. member for Niagara Falls is dealing now with a matter concerning an Indian agency, and concerning the operation and maintenance of one of these agencies. Next, the minister herself, when posed a question this afternoon, made it

quite clear she had no objection whatever to giving certain information to any hon. member in this house. The hon. member for Niagara Falls took advantage of that and got some information on the assumption, surely from what the minister said, that she would be able to discuss it tonight. Again, from what the minister said this evening, she indicated she had no objection to this matter being raised.
It seems to me, and I say this with respect, if there is a possibility, as I submit to you there is under this item, the hon. member should not have to wait until such time as the main estimates are up for discussion. Since the minister has at her disposal two of the officers of her department, it would seem to me there should be no objection on the part of the minister and I do not believe there is. I submit there should be none on the part of the Chair to the discussion of this item.

Mr. Chairman, possibly I could clarify the situation by saying that the vote under which this particular matter should come is that which is noted in the estimates as "Reserves and Trusts". It is vote No. 58 in the main estimates. The votes which are affected by these supplementaries are votes 56, 57, 59, 60, 61 and 63. I hope that clarifies the matter.

I take it, Mr. Chairman, I may discuss the matter which I raised.
This matter arose, Mr. Chairman, from the fact that about a year ago, in May, 1961, certain individuals in the province of British Columbia were interested in ascertaining whether or not there was in this particular reserve, which has been called Tsimpsean Indian reserve No. 2, timber available for cutting. Certain companies, or a company at least, began to write to the Indian affairs branch on the west coast and to the Ottawa offices with respect to it. I am informed that the timber in question had been offered by public calls for tenders on two earlier occasions, in 1954 and 1956. I believe the offer covered all the timber which was located in this particular area. However, at that time no offers were received. The stand of timber in question is of various types, Mr. Chairman. It is partly hemlock, partly spruce, partly balsam, partly cedar and is of varying grades.
In 1956 a certain company known as F. J. G. Johnson and Associates Limited of Vancouver was employed by the Indian affairs branch to do certain work with respect to this reserve and other reserves in British Columbia. He

recommended to the department a rate of dues to be charged on all of the Indian lands in British Columbia. Subsequently, in 1958, the Indian affairs branch hired this same company for a period of three years, on a one-year contract annually renewed, to cruise timber held by the Indians and thereby held in trust by the department, throughout British Columbia.
One of the chief individuals of this company is a man named F. J. G. Johnson. One of his employees during the time when the timber was being cruised by F. J. G. Johnson and Associates Limited for the department was a man named Brett, a man who now is employed by the department as a forestry officer in the city of Vancouver. Mr. Johnson was employed, through his limited company, until March 31, 1961. The day following, April 1, 1961, Mr. Paul Brett his former employee, was employed by the branch as a forester in British Columbia. Within a matter of a few weeks, certain companies began writing to the department to inquire about the sale of this timber. On May 18, a company known as Beaufort Industries Limited, Vancouver, wrote to the department in Vancouver asking whether this timber might be purchased. This was on May 18, 1961.
Within a matter of two weeks, May 30, 1961, Mr. F. J. G. Johnson, on the letterhead of his company, was writing to a number of companies, in particular the Westport Export Company of Vancouver, offering to peddle the information that he had obtained as an employee of the department. He offered to sell this information and indeed offered to ask, on a minimum fee basis, to negotiate the purchase of this timber from the department. He suggested that negotiations be conducted directly with the superintendent and the bands and chiefs council, with regard to Tsimpsean Indian reserve No. 2, which had previously been advertised for sale. He suggested that the regional office of the department of Indian affairs in Vancouver be approached-
May I ask the hon. member from what document she is reading?
I read from a photostat of a letter signed by F. J. G. Johnson on his letterhead. It is directed to the Westport Export Company.
To whom?
To the Westport Export Company.

May I ask further if this is a document which was gleaned from the files of the department?

I did not see it in the files of the department, if there is one there.
This timber was offered for sale, as I said, by Mr. Johnson who had, within the two months previously, terminated his employment with the department, on the basis of information which he learned as an employee.
He concludes his letter with this phrase, that every effort will be made to bring all negotiations to a speedy and successful conclusion. In addition I am informed that Mr. Johnson attempted to raise money in the United States to purchase timber rights on this particular land. In any event the company to which he wrote, Westport, was not interested in such a peculiar transaction and therefore refused.
At the same time Beaufort Industries Limited, which had written originally to the department, asked whether this timber was for sale and was advised that there were approximately 1 million board feet for sale, being virgin timber, over mature and lying approximately one mile from the sea. It was indicated in a letter written at that time, dated May 24, 1961, that such timber had been advertised previously but no offers had been received. It was suggested by the Indian superintendent, and a copy was sent to this individual, that Beaufort Industries Limited consult Mr. Paul Brett, the forester attached to the British Columbia office.
Subsequently Beaufort Industries was in consultation with the department and received a letter dated June 7, 1961, from the acting Indian commissioner for British Columbia, in which a quotation was made that there were approximately 113 million board feet of hemlock, spruce, cedar and balsam which was over mature. It also pointed out that logging chances were fair and that road and transport routes were difficult. It was further pointed out, and I read from page 2 of the letter:
The Indian affairs branch is presently interested in receiving competitive proposals to cut and remove the timber using Indian labour wherever possible.
Accordingly Beaufort, on invitation to submit a proposal, did so in writing. Before doing so they wrote to the department and asked it the department had any set figure, and under letter June 9, 1961, they enclosed a number of documents setting out the prices which had been paid in the immediate area for timber in recent months.
At this point I might say that Beaufort Industries Limited is a company of all Canadian directors and shareholders, located in Vancouver, and has been cutting timber for a long time in the Tsimpsean I.R. No. 2 reserve, in the reserve area, and cutting it very successfully. It has been exporting this
1726	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration timber to Japan, particularly low grade timber tor the construction of such things as orange fruit boxes.
When the had written to the department asking for prices they received a letter back again from Mr. MacGregor, the acting superintendent for British Columbia, on June 9, 1961, and he advised as follows:
We regret to advise you that the branch may not offer timber in the above quantities to individual companies. Ordinarily such timber is sold by closed tender on advertisement as a general offer to the public.
As it was pointed out to you, however, the branch cognizant of the particular local problems of the area, is receiving all competitive proposals to cut and remove the timber using Indian labour wherever possible.
This will indicate that while the department's usual practice was to request sealed bids, in this particular case since the branch knew of the local problems of the area individual offers were requested. Accordingly, after the passage of some time, in August, 1961, Beaufort Industries in writing sent to the Indian affairs branch in Vancouver a firm offer of $7 per 1,000 board feet of measure for all merchantable species. They indicated as well that they had intended to do this logging with Indian labour in all possible phases. In addition they offered to replant at the cost of the company to the same state as the original stand, concurrent with logging operations, and this would be done by Indian labour. They also offered that operations were to begin within 12 months and were to be completed within 10 years. They also offered a $25,000 deposit, which was the largest deposit required for provincial timber sales in British Columbia.
Subsequent to that firm offer which had been sent to the department in which Mr. Brett was the forester, and after a representative of that company had visited Ottawa and talked to representatives of the Indian affairs branch, they were informed that the department was designing a contract and proposal for the removal of the timber and subsequently it was the intent of the department to discuss it with Beaufort Industries and other interested companies with a view to the operation.
Subsequently by letter dated September 12, 1961, Beaufort Industries Limited made an addition to their offer which was to provide to the branch a maximum sum of $200,000, being $10,000 per year for each of two employees employed by the department, a community planning officer and a forest supervisor and co-ordinator, each of which officials should be employed and under the direct control of the department.
One of the proposals made by Beaufort would require a logging road, some 10 miles


in length, to be constructed from Fort Simpson, which is one of the dwelling places of the Indians, to an inlet called Tuck Inlet, whereby for the first time the Indians of that reserve would have safe passage from the northernmost parts of their reserve to the south and to Prince Rupert. As at present, these Indians are unable to travel through the land and must travel only by the Chatham sound, in very rough water and sometimes in very bad weather. However the road which Beaufort Industries was prepared to build- admittedly for its own purposes it was a logging road-would be good for at least 10 years, would remain the property of the Indians and would provide them with complete access through their reserve.
The Indian affairs branch, however, said that such a road could not or should not be built, notwithstanding the fact that the amount intended to be used was $500,000 by the Beaufort company. Indeed any proposal to build such a road would be entirely at the expense of the tenderer, and at no expense to the Indian affairs branch. Accordingly such an offer was made and, as I said before, there was an offer made to replant whatever timber was cut. This was done for two purposes, one to provide for effective regrowth, and second, to provide psychologically for the Indians by showing satisfactory proof to them that there would be no raping of their forests and that their children and grandchildren would again have forests to sell.
There was considerable discussion between representatives of Beaufort Industries Limited, and Mr. Paul Brett, the district forester, and he said that he recommended against reforestation. I am further advised that Mr. Johnson, who made the original cruise under the employment of the department, also recommend against reforestation and said it would regenerate naturally. In that connection it was interesting to listen to the remarks made during the last vote and hear those hon. members interested in forestry talking about the necessity of replanting; yet here we have a departmental forester who says it is not necessary to replant.
I am informed by a representative of the branch that in addition the forest officer in Ottawa checked with the executives of other companies with respect to this question of reforestation, as it became important later. We are now at the point where this firm bid has been put in writing to the department and has gone through Mr. Paul Brett's hands. Then there was a call for tenders made on September 15, 1961. It was sent out to the Beaufort company and to another company, Shoreline Lumber Limited. Shoreline Lumber Limited was, according to the

records of the registrar of companies in British Columbia, incorporated only on July 14, 1961. Its directors are most interesting. They are John C. Cotton, an American of Ashland, Oregon; Frederick J. G. Johnson, of North Vancouver, the same man employed by the department and the man who prepared the cruise map which is part of the tender; and Thomas E. Ladner, also of Vancouver, who I am informed is the son of one Leon Ladner, who is probably known to many of my hon. friends opposite as the chief fund raiser of the Conservative party in Vancouver. These three individuals incorporated a company in July of 1961. In December of 1961 the department issued its call for tenders. The original advertisement for tenders, and that which was sent to those who had become interested, said that tenders were to be handed in on January 16, but at the request of the Vancouver office-I am informed, at the particular request of Mr. Paul Brett, who as I pointed out was formerly an associate and employee of Mr. Johnson-it was delayed and the advertisement was changed to read for February 13. No notification was given to the Beaufort company that there had been a change in the date called for tenders.
On February 13 Beaufort's representative appeared in Ottawa with a written offer, and at the same time the offer of Shoreline Lumber Limited was received. The agent of Beaufort company was present with the officials of the department and the tenders were opened in his presence. He was told by the senior official opening the tenders that Beaufort had won the tender. In Beaufort's tender certain figures are produced. The department has made a point of the fact that it was not in the exact form of their original tender. In Beaufort's tender the price to be paid was $2,237,925. This sum was in cash and in kind and is set out in a separate memorandum attached. With the offer sent in by Beaufort was their certified cheque for more than $59,000 as was required in the offer. The only other bid that was received was from Shoreline Lumber Limited, which totalled $792,000 plus some fringe benefits.
When one reduces the items to indicate exactly what was offered, one finds that Beaufort had offered certain upset prices plus other sums, $200,000 of which they were prepared to pay to the department for economic development for the Indians, plus the value of the $500,000 road which would be a permanent benefit to the Indians, plus the fact that they were bidding not on the timber which was shown only on the map prepared by Mr. Johnson at the behest of the department and upon which Mr. Johnson had bid, 26207-1-110
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration but in fact upon low grade timber as well, which would have brought an additional cash benefit to the Indians.
When the tender was first put out it contained an interesting provision, which was that it was the desire of the department that Indians on this reserve should gain maximum benefit from this sale, including the opportunity to acquire skill, and other permanent benefits. Under the Beaufort bid they would have obtained cash for the sale of considerably more timber than under the accepted bid. They would in addition have obtained a permanent road, two permanent employees for 10 years, and they would have had considerably more timber cut.
Not insignificant is the fact that with the road they would have had a certain safety factor which does not now exist. In addition to this they would have had employment and the additional benefit of having the forest replanted. However, notwithstanding the fact that on February 13, 1961, Beaufort was advised that it had won the contract as high tenderer, under the date of February 21, 1961, they received a telegram from the officer in charge of reserves and trusts in Ottawa saying that they were a low tenderer, that Shoreline Lumber Limited was high tenderer and had won the bid. On the same date their cheque was returned to them. This was confirmed by letter.
On the same date Mr. Boys, the Indian commissioner for British Columbia, wrote to Chief Sampson of the band and advised him that the department had accepted a conditional tender. In fact the tender which was accepted from Shoreline-this is the company with Johnson and Ladner and this American- contains the proviso that the tender is submitted on the understanding that logs removed from this Indian reserve would be allowed to be exported, and if to the contrary the bid was withdrawn.
This to me, and it must be to many hon. members in this house, is a considerable shock, that when two tenders are placed before the department, the department accepts a conditional tender. This was repeated, as I said, in the letter which was written by Mr. Boys to Chief Sampson, where the price which had been paid was indicated and also that the earliest start of logging activity would be the spring of 1963. This very important proviso was also contained in the tender:
In addition Shoreline Lumber Limited do not intend to execute the contract until such time as they secure a permit to export the timber, where approval of this matter will not unduly delay the project.
An interesting thing occurred. In so far as the Shoreline bid was concerned there was a very detailed plan with respect to the economic development of the Indians and it was

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the opinion of the Indian affairs branch that this company, which had never been in existence before last July, knew considerably more about the Indians on this reserve than anyone else. In fact it should be remembered that Mr. Johnson-and Mr. Brett had been associated with Mr. Johnson-the chief forester of the Vancouver office, had been sent by the department to the reserve in the fall of last year with another gentleman, Mr. Addison, who is the chief placement officer for British Columbia, where apparently they drew up an economic proposal. That economic proposal, being one which is solely within departmental jurisdiction, is not available. Therefore there can only be speculation as to how closely that proposal parallels the proposal which turned up in Johnson's bid which was accepted.
I should like to once more draw the attention of hon. members to the stunning regularity with which Mr. Johnson's and Mr. Brett's names come up again and again. Mr. Johnson had been Mr. Brett's employer. Mr. Johnson did the cruise in 1959 in this timber reserve. On March 31, 1961, Mr. Johnson left the department. The next day, April 1, Mr. Brett was hired. Mr. Johnson recommended the dues to be charged. Mr. Brett recommended the upset prices. Both recommended that there be no reforestation planning. Mr. Johnson tried to sell the timber to other individuals. Mr. Johnson was a member of the company which was incorporated. Mr. Brett was the one who at the tenderer's request delayed the job for call of tender. Mr. Brett went to the reserve to look up the economic problem, and Mr. Brett saw all the correspondence at all times.
This could be a matter of argument between businessmen, but it would appear that all of the gentlemen concerned are supporters of the party of the hon. lady opposite. There are no supporters of my party, or at least there were not until relatively recently, among these individuals. I would suggest, however, that this is not simply a matter of two individuals one, by virtue of honest bids one against the other, having won, and the other having lost. There is a definite pattern of collusion by an employee of the Indian affairs branch with a former employee. This government has from time to time made a great thing of the fact that-

Mr. Chairman, I have hesitated to interrupt the hon. lady although she has been out of order for half an hour, but I do say now that I cannot sit here and let her accuse members of my department of collusion. I ask her to withdraw that remark.
