Mr. Chairman, I would like to impress upon the minister in charge of this department the utmost importance of having this situation with regard to the selling of timber on the reserves in British Columbia clarified as speedily and as completely as possible. If that is not done almost immediately the effect in British Columbia will be most serious, not just upon the Indians on the reserve but as far as the native Indians of the entire province are concerned.
This matter was drawn emphatically to my attention this morning when at 9.00 o'clock a telegram was delivered to me signed by the chief of the council of the Indians of this particular reserve. I found it almost impossible to believe the information which was contained in that telegram, which stated that as between two tenders for certain timber limits there was a difference between them of almost $2 million in one instance and less than $1 million in the other, and that the bidder offering less than $1 million had been awarded the tender. The Indians, through their chief, had been unanimous in objecting to this type of operation and to this policy and had asked that the matter be investigated immediately. Having received a telegram of that nature I took what I thought was the correct procedure. I at once telephoned the Indian affairs branch to read the telegram to them and ask for whatever information could be given to me. It was about 9.20 this morning when the departmental official told me of the situation. I was asking for information because this telegram had to be answered. I was amazed to be told that the basic information contained in the telegram, was correct. Then the statement was made that the Indian affairs branch was only interested in one thing, namely, to ensure that in the long run as a result of the actions and policies of the department the greatest amount of money and benefit would accrue to the Indians concerned. It was stated that studies had led the branch to believe that in giving the tender to the applicant who had made the lower bid the Indians on this reserve would get the greater amount of money. That was very confusing to me, so I ask hon. members of this committee to

imagine how much more difficult still it would be for the Indians themselves to understand.
Then I was given additional information, and I appreciate the fact that I was given it. I was told that there were a number of differences or discrepancies in the way the tenders were handled. I was told that the tenderer putting in the highest bid-it happened to be the Beaufort people, I believe- had tendered on the basis of six or eight thousand acres of timber which was not to be sold. Without going into detail, I was given to understand that there were two or three other aspects having to do with reforestation. In addition, there was a question of roads. In all, there were a number of matters which were of such a nature that the Indian affairs branch had asked the forestry department for an analysis, and that on the basis of this analysis and the recommendation of a forestry official-I did not get his name, and I do not know it now-this particular decision was reached.
I think, Mr. Chairman, you will agree that at least on the surface this decision does not make sense. It has got to make sense, or there is something wrong. The Indians in British Columbia must have an answer, and they are entitled to that answer now. The only way they can get it is for a presentation to be made by the minister explaining this paradoxical situation and explaining how, according to this decision of the department, the Indians concerned are going to receive the greatest ultimate benefit in services or money.
I shall not continue to make any of the other observations I may have in mind at the present time. The minister knows about this matter; she knows there are some of us who are interested in it, and surely she expected it to be raised. I am going to sit down now, for a few minutes at least, in the hope that the minister will make a start, at least, toward clearing the air and telling the committee the facts behind this extraordinary situation in connection with this timber on the coast of British Columbia.

Before the minister replies I should like to address a few further questions to her on this subject. Perhaps the minister will advise the committee how it is that the offer made in writing by Beaufort last fall to the department in the amount of $791,000 is so peculiarly close to the offer made by the successful tenderer of $792,000. Perhaps the minister will also tell us how it is that such a conditional offer was accepted by the department. Perhaps she will tell us, as well, how it is that when the department in its tender call said it would not necessarily accept the highest or any bid it did not 26207-1-110J
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration include certain timber, about 8,000 acres, as the hon. member for Vancouver East has just stated, which had been previously included in two sales offered in 1954 and 1956.
I was today informed by the department that this timber cannot be sold because it was not offered. Yet the same official admitted to me that if it was not sold as one parcel it would never be sold because it would be completely uneconomic to go in and cut low grade timber once the better timber had been taken out.
If this sale is allowed to stand, the birthright of the Indians on this one reserve is going to be reduced by over $1 million because this timber will never be sold. Further, the $500,000 which was to be spent to connect the Indian settlements by a safe passage by road will never be spent-
Nonsense.

I do hope the hon. member who said that has looked at the actual contract before crying "nonsense", very much as the Minister of Finance does when anyone stands up in this house. This is not nonsense. The successful bid means there will be three miles of haul road built in from the sea to the heart of the good timber; it goes nowhere near the Indian settlements; it will be of no permanent value at all.
Perhaps the minister can tell us why this is not a firm contract for ten years but only a contract for one year renewable for up to ten years under certain conditions. The successful bidder can get out of the contract if he chooses in certain circumstances, these too having been accepted by the government. All these people have to do is say: we cannot get an export permit. And they do not even have to apply for one. Why is it that the minister, having accepted this bid, has decided to wait and see. I suggest to the minister that if the department knows there is someone interested in purchasing all the timber-and if it has known this since last September-the bids should be recalled and the department should ask for the sale of all the timber on the reserve. I ask the minister to check the peculiar report prepared by the officials of her department in British Columbia against the particulars of the successful tender. I invite the minister to ask herself about the relationship between these two people unless, of course, the hon. lady is not prepared to ask herself because of the fact that there is an American at the head of this company and Mr. Ladner is on the board of directors.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I do not think the hon. lady is entitled to smear a gentleman of her own

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration profession simply because he happens to be named to the board of directors of a company. I am sure the hon. lady in her career as a lawyer has frequently been named to the boards of directors of companies.

Mr. Chairman, I did not say anything about him except that he happened to be one of the directors. If my hon. friend thinks it is a smear to be a director of a lumber company it may be because he has certain further information I do not have.
However, Mr. Chairman, there is one principle concerned. The hon. lady throughout her career has expressed a considerable interest in Indians. All hon. members realize that many of these people are in need of considerable help, that many of them in such isolated places must rely on the good faith of the department, the officers of which are trustees for them, in ensuring that these funds when received are put aside for their benefit. Any training program set up is established by the department for their good. They are used as labour and are trained as far as possible to be skilled labourers. The hon. lady must appreciate that in terms of the following resolution which came forward and which I wish to read to the committee that necessary confidence between this band and the Indian affairs branch is completely destroyed.
This resolution was unanimously passed by band members of the Tsimpsean Indian reserve No. 2 and is dated March 7, 1962. It reads as follows:
1.	Regarding the sale of our timber on Indian reserve No. 2 we hereby agree to accept the offer of the company that tendered on February 13, 1962 to build a road from Tuck inlet to Port Simpson as we regard this road as being of the utmost importance to the band's well-being.
2.	We further agree to accept this company's offer to replant the areas that are cut and we consider this most important as it will give additional work to members of this band now and to future generations.
3.	We further agree to accept this company's offer to remove all the merchantable timber from the reserve at the same price that was offered for the high grade timber and we know that this will substantially increase the cash amount paid to us over any other offer for high grade areas only.
4.	We understand that this company's offer is for a ten year period and we will not accept an offer for any lesser period.
In summary, we understand that a tender has been tentatively accepted by the department of Indian affairs in Ottawa that does not include all of the foregoing mentioned in paragraphs 1 to 4 and we are shocked to find that the offer tentatively accepted by the department of Indian affairs was binding for one year only and was for a much smaller amount of timber and had no provisions for replanting or building our vitally needed access and logging road. We feel that some members of the department of Indian affairs are definitely not acting in the best interests of the

members of this band and this council now unanimously agrees not to accept any offer that does not contain:
1.	Access road from Tuck inlet to Fort Simpson-
That is not in the successful tender.
2.	Replanting of areas cut-
That is not in the successful tender.
3.	Cutting the largest areas possible and removing the largest amount of timber which will return to the band the greatest amount of money.
That is not in the successful tender.
4.	A firm ten-year period.
That is also not in the successful tender. This resolution is signed by the chief and secretary of the band and by six other band members. It is critically important that the minister look into this matter now, that in fact she be able to satisfy herself that it is a proper tender, that she be able to satisfy herself that the Indians who are her charges are the ones who will be benefited and benefited most. I would suggest to the minister that notwithstanding what I am advised by the department it is not necessary to have a surrender with respect to such a one-year contract. I am further informed by the department that there is an old surrender on these lands and that it is not necessary to have the Indians' consent.
I do not know very much about the members of the band on this reserve but I am told that in earlier times they tore up stakes and went after white men who came on the reserve. It is extremely important that their trust be restored. It is also important that the best type of cutting operation possible, be carried out on this reserve and I suggest to the minister that this be done.
There is one small matter in which it appears that the department may or may not have been negligent and that is during the fall of last year. After Beaufort was in contact with the department a notice appeared in the British Columbia Gazette that another company-I am not positive of its name but I believe it is Prince Rupert Saw Mill-had applied for a licence on foreshore rights on the inlet called Tuck inlet which is the egress ultimately to the sea and which Beaufort intended and had advised the department they intended to use to take out timber, if they were successful in obtaining this bid. It was Beaufort that brought to the attention of the department the fact that anyone who obtained foreshore rights would in fact be giving the Indians access ultimately to the ocean.
There is another significant fact about which the hon. lady may wish to inquire. Why is it that the map prepared by Johnson and associates for the department at the department's expense, which expense, of

course, is reimbursed to the person who successfully tenders, had removed from it the legend showing Mr. Johnson's name? Why is it that when one examines the map one finds a raw edge and the place where the legend normally would appear does not show? It was only when I was able to obtain the original map today that I was able to ascertain that it was in fact the map prepared by Johnson.
Now, if the hon. lady is not alarmed by some of the facts brought out today, if she is quiescent and feels there is nothing to this, that it is simply a complaint taken to the opposition by individuals who unjustifiably feel themselves aggrieved, I can only say that the hon. lady has no business being the trustee for the Indians.

Mr. Chairman, although it is almost ten o'clock perhaps I may be permitted to say a few words in view of the fact that the hon. member has occupied almost an hour. My remarks will be very brief. I wish first of all to point out that this item is not one which is in the estimates for consideration today. The question comes under vote No. 58 relating to reserves and trusts and is not contained in these supplementary estimates.
Earlier in the day the hon. member addressed a question to the Prime Minister in reply to which I advised that I had already ordered an investigation into this matter. I might tell the hon- member and the committee that I ordered this investigation prior to March 7, the date of the resolution from the Indian band to which the hon. lady directed our attention. I also pointed out this afternoon that Mr. Boys, the commissioner for British Columbia, will be visiting the Tsimp-sean reserve to morrow. After his visit there when the report has been received I will make a report to this house. I reiterate, Mr. Chairman, that this whole discussion thus far has been related to an item which is not even under consideration this evening.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
Resolution adopted in committee of supply this day reported and concurred in.
Business of the House BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the
house leader what we will be doing tomorrow and Wednesday?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I hope we will be able to complete the supplementary estimates tomorrow, Mr. Speaker, and we could do so, I think, if we gave very close attention to the items that are called. If we do not complete them tomorrow, we will of course have to continue with the supplementary estimates on Wednesday because, as I pointed out to the house last week, certain projects will have to be discontinued for lack of money to carry them on and certain people will go without their pay because the money has not been voted by parliament. I think we have now spent about 10 days on these supplementary estimates and should get on expeditiously with the business tomorrow.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On that point, Mr. Speaker, we have not spent anything like 10 days on these supplementary estimates-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We have. We had five days in January on them.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -as the minister has said. In any event, I do not think it is up to the minister to lecture the house on the manner in which these estimates are going to be dealt with by the opposition. We will deal with them in the manner in which we feel they should be dealt with in the best interests of the country.
Obstruction.

It being three minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
